articles.title: ‘There will never be another Dolly’: Tributes to Parton pour in across generations
articles.summary: Entertainers and celebrities reflected on Parton’s creative talent, while fans and everyday people recounted how her philanthropic generosity touched their lives.
articles.body: Reflecting the magnitude of her influence and impact, Dolly Parton’s death drew immediate tributes from across industries, genres, generations, places and people. Entertainers, film stars, politicians and everyday people who benefited from her generosity and her enterprises quickly filled social media with their stories of how she improved their lives, how her songs uplifted or taught them, how she made them laugh and how they just loved who she was. The accolades poured in from around the globe, offered up from sources as varied as country music superstars Reba McEntire, Kacey Musgraves and Linda Ronstadt to Khloe Kardashian and the Muppets, as well as singers and other celebrities, including Mick Jagger, Dionne Warwick, Pink, Keke Palmer, Lily Tomlin, Kelly Clarkson, Amazon founder Jeff Bezos and fashion designer Donatella Versace. President Donald Trump ordered flags lowered for a week, writing on Truth Social, “There has never been anyone like her, and there never will,” as politicians from both sides of the aisle paid tribute. Former President Bill Clinton wrote on social media that Parton was “one of a kind — a great songwriter and performer who told the stories of everyday Americans with honesty, humility, and heart. She rose high from her East Tennessee roots and never forgot where she came from.” McEntire wrote of getting the news that “my buddy Dolly passed onto the higher and greater side.” She thanked her for “all the wonderful things you did for us here on earth” and said, “There will never ever be another you.” Some of country music’s royalty sang her praises and were joined by a younger generation of musicians and songwriters who heralded her as an inspiration. “This really hurts,” wrote Musgraves, a multiple Grammy award winner. Parton drew an homage from the “King of Country Music,” George Strait, who said on Facebook: “You’ve had such a huge impact all over the world, @dollyparton. We will all miss you. May God bless the Parton family.” The adoration was not confined to country music. “She was a sweet and kind soul and I’m proud to say I knew her. ... There will never be another Dolly,” said Gene Simmons, bassist and co-founder of the hard rock band Kiss. The Muppets posted a black-and-white photo of Parton with Miss Piggy, saying, “She filled the world with light and we are so grateful for every second we got to spend with her onstage and off.” Comedian Lily Tomlin, Parton’s longtime friend, wrote, “No words...” followed by a broken heart emoji, alongside a black-and-white photo of the two, side by side with large smiles. In a video reel, Tomlin featured photos of herself with Jane Fonda, who co-starred with them in the 1980s hit “9 to 5.” Parton’s title song for the 1980 movie — which topped the Billboard country chart — played in the background. National Organization for Women President Kim Villanueva said in a statement that Parton “defined feminism,” adding that her role in “9 to 5” emphasized that women in the workplace “deserved to be treated equally and with respect.” “She encouraged women to embrace who they wanted to be and stand up for their values,” Villanueva wrote. Donna Brazile, the former chair of the Democratic National Convention, posted that Parton “spent decades quietly funding band uniforms and instruments at Black high schools across the South — never once putting her name on it. No headlines, no fanfare — just help, given because it was needed.” Meanwhile, Rep. Tim Burchett, a Republican from Tennessee, Parton’s native state, said the state had lost one of its greatest ambassadors, who represented “the very best of the American dream.” Parton’s music “inspired generations of Americans and her philanthropic work helped provide greater access to education for countless young Tennesseans,” he said. Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer, D-N.Y., wrote on X, “Rest in peace, Dolly Parton — a true legend and a force for good.” Parton’s Dollywood Foundation focused on improving children’s educational success and stemming dropout rates in Tennessee. It gave birth to Dolly Parton’s Imagination Library, which sent books to children around the world. Her work was inspired by her father’s illiteracy. A father who said he’s in Australia posted on X that his young daughter got her first book Monday night from Parton’s Imagination Library. All of his children read it with their mother and laughed and enjoyed it, he said. The Library of Congress posted a photo of Parton, with reading glasses, conducting a story time book reading to children at the library. It described her as a “titan of children’s literacy” and said she donated the 100 millionth book to its collection. Parton helped fund crucial infectious disease research, with Scientific American paying tribute to her for her $1 million donation to Vanderbilt University Medical Center in Nashville, Tennessee, to help fund an early-stage trial of the Covid vaccine in 2020. She told NBC News that she donated to the vaccine effort because “I just wanted to do good.” She also helped promote Covid vaccinations with a video of her getting the shot and an adjustment to her song “Jolene” to “Vaccine.” The Motion Picture Academy awarded her its Jean Hersholt Humanitarian Award last year. Dollywood, Parton’s much-beloved theme park in Pigeon Forge, Tennessee, will open Wednesday. “In her spirit, Dollywood will be open Wednesday as Dolly wanted, always reminding everyone with her signature sparkle — ‘the show must go on,’” the company said in a statement. “Together, we honor her by carrying forward her message of love, perseverance and hope.”

articles.title: Creator ties AI data centers to water crisis, offers state-by-state legal safeguards
articles.summary: "What most people don't know is that access to water and a healthful environment is a right!"
articles.body:
An Instagram creator's recent reel explained that water scarcity is not only about dwindling resources.

The creator urged viewers to learn what legal safeguards exist in their states as AI and data centers place mounting strain on water supplies.

In a post shared on Aug. 19, Instagram creator Ayana Gray (@ayana.g123) addressed the growing tension between public water supplies and the AI data center boom.

Gray linked shrinking water supplies to several pressures, including "increased heat, general human industrial activity, and of course, data centers and AI."

"The water crisis is already happening, and this is just the beginning," she warned.

Data centers support everything from chatbots to cloud storage, but they require large amounts of electricity and their cooling systems often depend on significant water use, especially in hot or drought-prone regions.

Rather than focusing solely on expansion and permitting, the post emphasized legal rights related to environmental conditions.

"What most people don't know is that access to water and a healthful environment is a right! It's a right we must protect," Gray wrote.

The poster also asked followers to name their states in the comments so she could respond with information about local laws.

"For more information on your state's position on the right to a healthful environment, respond with the name of your state and I will reply to you about your state's laws!" she said.

Concern over AI's environmental footprint goes beyond water alone.

These tools run on energy-intensive chips housed in data centers, placing new demand on the power grid, which is already being asked to handle rising cooling demand, electric vehicles , and industrial expansion.

AI can help utilities balance electricity demand, improve building efficiency, accelerate clean energy planning, and support more accurate forecasting for solar and wind.

However, those potential benefits exist alongside real risks, including high electricity and cooling needs, cybersecurity concerns, misuse, and higher utility costs if infrastructure expands faster than cleaner power supplies do.

When large industrial users move into a community, residents often worry about whether local water supplies will remain dependable during hotter, drier periods and whether the burdens and benefits are being shared fairly.

States vary widely in how they approach environmental rights, water protections, and industrial permitting.

Gray's invitation for people to comment with their state names exposed a worrisome truth: Many people do not know what legal protections exist where they live.

Public hearings, water-use plans, energy-sourcing disclosures, and utility filings can reveal whether a project is expected to rely heavily on local water supplies or strain the grid.

Policymakers and utilities can require greater transparency around how AI infrastructure uses power and water.

Stronger reporting, more efficient cooling systems, cleaner electricity procurement, and better planning can help reduce some of the pressure these facilities place on communities.

articles.title: Pennsylvania attorney general accuses Snapchat of failing to protect children in new lawsuit
articles.summary: Pennsylvania Attorney General Dave Sunday (R) announced a lawsuit Tuesday, accusing Snap, the parent company of Snapchat, of failing to protect children from...
articles.body:
Pennsylvania Attorney General Dave Sunday (R) announced a lawsuit Tuesday, accusing Snap, the parent company of Snapchat, of failing to protect children from compulsively using its platform.

The complaint , filed this week, alleges Snapchat knowingly lies about the frequency of adult-themed material like drug use or sexual content to maintain a 13+ app rating in app stores.

"Once they have you signed up and logged in, you are officially in their clutches," the attorney general said at a press conference Tuesday. "From there, Snapchat essentially says good luck getting out."

Sunday said he hopes for "honesty" from Snapchat, accusing the company's actions of violating Pennsylvania's consumer protection laws.

"The lawsuit also demands that Snapchat finally come clean about the addictiveness of their app and takes real action to protect young users," Sunday said. "This is a very serious legal action with the end goals of being an overhaul of how Snapchat markets and advertises its app."

Sunday alleged Snapchat uses functions like the Snap Streak feature, which counts the number of days two users send Snaps to one another to keep users engaged. The streak is lost when one of the users does not Snap the other in 24 hours.

"We allege this streak feature puts a tangible value on friendships and influences a child's feelings of self-worth," he said.

Sunday also argued that Snapchat's disappearing stories, messages and photos encourage users to post things they may typically not, like a revealing selfie.

The state prosecutor said parents do not have time to "fully explore" every platform and relies on "transparency" from companies when making decisions about their children's social media use.

A spokesperson for Snap stated that the allegations "fundamentally misrepresent" the platform and its approach to teen safety.

"Snapchat was designed differently from the beginning: it opens to a camera, not a feed of content, and was built to encourage self-expression and authentic connection with friends," the spokesperson told The Hill.

"We share the Attorney General's commitment to protecting young people online and are disappointed they have chosen litigation rather than working with us toward that shared goal," the spokesperson continued.

Sunday's suit comes just weeks after he announced a complaint against TikTok over similar allegations .

As the committee met, Maken raised the issue and was supported by a number of other opposition MPs, including Priyanka and Senta UBTâs Sanjay Raut. They said the Delhi Police chief should be asked to appear before the committee, insisting that the issue fell within the ambit of crimes against children.Agrawal said the matter is sub judice. With opposition MPs pressing their demand, BJP MP Tarun Chugh said that if members are allowed to raise issues not on the agenda, then he would like the committee to take up the alleged glorification of a Sikh-riots convict, a reference to former Congress MP Sajjan Kumar who died last week while serving his sentence.Chughâs remarks drew a sharp reaction from Congress MP Jai Prakash, who said the issue was not relevant at all. articles.title: Prominent Sikh separatist says FBI has warned him of new threat on his life
articles.summary: A prominent Sikh separatist said Tuesday that the FBI and the Royal Canadian Mounted Police have warned him that he faces a new credible threat to his life e...
articles.body:
NEW YORK (AP) — A prominent Sikh separatist said Tuesday that the FBI and the Royal Canadian Mounted Police have warned him that he faces a new credible threat to his life even as a man from India faces sentencing later this year for a 2023 death plot against him.

Gurpatwant Singh Pannun, general counsel for Sikhs For Justice, said he was warned by FBI agents who visited him last Thursday that he should not travel until the threat is resolved, and, if he does, the agency should be notified in advance of his plans.

He said the Royal Canadian Mounted Police warned him by telephone on Tuesday, though neither law enforcement agency gave any details about the plot that was uncovered. Messages seeking comment from both law enforcement agencies were not immediately returned.

Pannun, a dual U.S.-Canadian citizen, said he was warned according to the terms of a "Duty to Warn" law in the United States that obligates U.S. intelligence and law enforcement agencies to notify individuals when they discover credible and specific threats of murder, severe bodily harm or kidnapping.

The new threat comes as Nikhil Gupta, a man from India who pleaded guilty to federal conspiracy charges in February, awaits a Nov. 20 sentencing in Manhattan federal court for plotting in 2023 with others to assassinate Pannun.

The FBI has said Gupta was directed by an Indian government employee to carry out the killing. When Gupta tried, he unwittingly communicated with an undercover law enforcement officer posing as a hitman. Federal sentencing guidelines call for Gupta to spend at least two decades in prison.

Pannun, who advocates for the creation of the sovereign Sikh state and is considered a terrorist by the Indian government, said in a phone interview Tuesday that he was "unfazed and undaunted" by the attempts to silence him.

"I'm not afraid of their death threats," he said, though he added that he hoped that the administrations of President Donald Trump and Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney would confront Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi over threats to U.S. and Canadian sovereignty.

"The Modi government is proceeding under the Trump administration without fear of any consequences," he said.

Pannun has described himself as a Sikh human rights lawyer who is campaigning to turn Punjab into a place where "all religions will have equal rights."

He said "Duty to Warn" advisories were issued by Canadian law enforcement officials to Hardeep Singh Nijjar, the ex-head of the Canadian chapter of the Khalistan Referendum, in the weeks before he was assassinated on June 18, 2023 in Surrey, British Columbia.

Pannun said the continued threats give him courage and confidence that his campaign and outspokenness is working.

"I'm going to continue, even at the cost of a bullet," he said.

articles.title: Abandoned vans lead deputies to $123K in Brooks shoes from BNSF boxcar theft
articles.summary: Deputies traveling toward Ludlow found two abandoned vehicles matching descriptions from the rail investigation. BNSF police confirmed boxes inside came from...
articles.body:
California deputies recovered more than $123,000 in Brooks running shoes after a suspected BNSF train boxcar burglary. San Bernardino County deputies found two abandoned vans while traveling toward Ludlow on Aug. 22. BNSF Railway Police had requested assistance after a train made an emergency stop nearby. Authorities had noticed three vehicles near the train under suspicious circumstances.

Deputies inspected both vans and discovered numerous boxes inside each vehicle. BNSF Police confirmed the boxes came from the boxcar, according to the San Bernardino County Sheriff's Department announcement . Authorities identified the recovered merchandise as Brooks running shoes. The department valued the footwear at more than $123,000.

The incident occurred near Ludlow and Daggett in San Bernardino County, California. Those communities sit along National Trails Highway in the High Desert. BNSF Police asked deputies to help investigate the suspected burglary after the emergency stop. Deputies then spotted two vehicles matching the description of vehicles near the rail equipment.

"Deputies inspected the vans, discovering numerous boxes inside each of them," the sheriff's department wrote. "Upon examination, BNSF Police confirmed the boxes contained were from the boxcar." The announcement does not identify the train's origin or destination. Officials also did not describe how the boxes left the railcar.

FreightWaves requested comment and additional information from BNSF Railway but had not received a response by publication. The sheriff's department has not identified suspects or announced arrests. Authorities did not name the owners of the abandoned vehicles. The announcement does not state whether deputies recovered all missing merchandise. The investigation remains open.

Anyone with information can contact Sheriff's Dispatch at 760-956-5001. Anonymous callers can call or text REPORT to We-Tip at 844-909-3006. The sheriff's department also provided an online reporting option . FreightWaves requested additional information from BNSF Railway Police and will update this story if officials respond.

Rail theft can move high-value freight out of the supply chain before a shipper, buyer or carrier identifies the loss. This case shows how quickly merchandise can leave rail equipment and enter vehicles on the ground. Fast reporting and coordination between railroad police and local law enforcement can improve recovery efforts.

articles.title: A Montana man killed 8 relatives, including 4 kids, at Sunday dinner, a family spokesperson says
articles.summary: A man killed eight of his relatives, including four children, at a Sunday dinner at a home in Billings, Montana, before taking his own life, a spokesperson f...
articles.body:
A man killed eight of his relatives, including four children, at a Sunday dinner at a home in Billings, Montana, before taking his own life, a spokesperson for the family told The Associated Press.

Jennifer Mercer, who set up an online fundraiser to help cover funeral costs and other expenses and was authorized to release details, identified the victims as representing four generations of the blended family, ranging from a great-grandmother in her 90s to a 7-year-old girl.

Police said they responded to the home on Sunday evening and heard gunshots coming from out back, just before the house was completely engulfed in flames. They confirmed multiple fatalities, including one person with a self-inflicted gunshot wound.

David Hiller, a neighbor who lives three doors down from the home, heard what he thought were fireworks just after 6 p.m. on Sunday, and didn't think much of the noise until another neighbor called to warn him about a shooting on the cul-de-sac.

Hiller then rushed outside to find police in tactical gear sheltering behind vehicles, some with long guns, while plumes of black smoke rose from the home.

articles.title: What we know about Southwest flight attendant's death in Hawaii
articles.summary: Authorities say no conclusions have been made in the death of Southwest flight attendant Jenny Lupton as Honolulu detectives continue investigating.
articles.body:
The investigation into the death of a Southwest Airlines flight attendant in Waikiki has entered a new phase, with Honolulu police confirming that the department's Homicide Detail is now leading the inquiry.

Jenny Lupton, 50, of Moore, Oklahoma, was found dead on Aug. 20 while on a work layover in Honolulu. The Honolulu Police Department said Aug. 24 that detectives are actively investigating the circumstances surrounding her death but emphasized that they have not confirmed how she died.

Police said investigators are conducting interviews, reviewing and recovering surveillance video and working closely with Lupton's family. Authorities also urged the public to rely on verified information as the investigation continues.

Southwest Airlines confirmed Lupton's death to USA TODAY on Aug. 24, saying she died while in Hawaii during a layover.

Her niece, Hannah Lupton, told USA TODAY that the Honolulu Department of the Medical Examiner informed the family it appeared her aunt fell from the balcony of her 24th-floor room at the Hilton Hawaiian Village in Waikiki. She was found near a contamination bin below the balcony.

Lupton's family has continued to press for answers, saying they do not believe she died by suicide.

USA TODAY contacted the Honolulu Medical Examiner's Office and the Honolulu Police Department for additional information on Aug. 25. Officials have said Lupton's cause and manner of death remain pending.

Why is the Homicide Detail investigating?

The Honolulu Police Department said its Homicide Detail is leading the investigation because the unit handles homicides as well as suspicious, unattended and other unexplained deaths.

Police emphasized that assigning the case to the Homicide Detail does not indicate Lupton's death has been ruled a homicide. Officials said investigators won't publicly discuss additional details because the inquiry is ongoing.

Lupton's family has voiced concerns about the flight attendant's unexpected death.

"We are worried that there is possible foul play involved," Hannah Lupton previously told USA TODAY. Officials have not publicly said they suspect a specific cause.

Her sister, Tresa Lupton, told Oklahoma-based television station KFOR that the family believes she either died after "some kind of freak accident or someone harmed her."

Hannah Lupton also described her aunt as "the life of the party," saying she loved her family, her 15-year-old son and her hometown of Moore, Oklahoma.

A GoFundMe campaign set up by Lupton's coworkers to assist her family had raised over $10,900 toward a $26,000 goal as of Aug. 25.

Police have not announced a timeline for completing the investigation, saying it "will take time" as detectives continue gathering evidence.

Lupton's family plans to travel to Hawaii to bring her body home to Oklahoma and work with officials.

The office of the Oklahoma Attorney General Gentner Drummond said it has been in contact with the Hawaii Attorney General to help ensure a thorough investigation and remains in communication with Lupton's family, who "deserve to have answers about this tragedy."

Southwest Airlines said in a statement that it is "engaged with local authorities as they investigate" and has offered its condolences to Lupton's family and coworkers.

articles.title: Michael Sheen toxic waste documentary 'the tip of the iceberg'
articles.summary: One scientist says there are thousands of sites across the UK that need investigating.
articles.body:
A former Monsanto worker who spent three years helping seal toxic waste underground said staff had "cheap" protective equipment and were not told what they were burying.

Stephen Constance worked at the chemical giant's Newport factory in the 1990s and came forward after the BBC documentary Buried with Michael Sheen highlighted Wales' toxic waste legacy.

But the 14 sites identified in the programme are just the tip of the iceberg and there are about 20,000 high-concern sites in the UK, said Dr David Megson, the scientist involved in the documentary.

Eastman Chemical Company, which is responsible for Monsanto's legacy production in the UK, did not respond when asked to comment.

Constance was one of dozens of people who contacted BBC Wales after coverage of Sheen's investigation into Monsanto and the dumping of polychlorinated biphenyls (PCBs).

Researcher and whistleblower Douglas Gowan spent 50 years trying to persuade authorities to investigate what he believed was widespread dumping of industrial chemicals.

These included PCBs, which he called "some of the worst contaminants known to man", and were widely used in the 20th Century, including for lipstick and white goods.

They were banned in the UK in the 1970s and have since been banned by 151 countries.

Constance, 61, said working for Monsanto was "absolutely dreadful".

Looking back, he said it was "quite evident that nobody was fully appraised of the potential hazard that they were exposed to".

The material was already buried when Constance arrived and it was his job to dig a 6m-deep trench around the outside of the mound before it was sealed using plastic membrane sheets and liquid clay.

While he believes this prevented airborne contamination, he is unsure if it would have stopped contamination into the Earth due to the high water table linked to the tides.

When asked if he felt safe, he said: "In terms of what we knew was there and what we were potentially exposed to, no."

Constance is in remission from cancer after having follicular lymphoma .

"I'm not suggesting in any way at all that it's linked, but the thought did cross my mind," he said.

In the documentary, journalists Dan Ashby and Lucy Taylor reveal a memo from Monsanto dated to 1972 which found that it knew PCBs were a danger to human health and was closing its site in the US as a result of legal action from a town.

However, it then increased its work at the plant in Newport.

"The government in the UK told the industry 'we're not going to put any restrictions on importing PCBs'," said Ashby.

"So they begin importing from around the world, hundreds of tonnes of PCBs."

Dr Megson, a reader in chemistry and environmental forensics at Manchester Metropolitan University, led the scientific data collection in the documentary.

He said: "The country is in a really dire place.

"Public pressure is the only thing that's going to make this action happen. This is our only chance, if I'm being brutally honest.

"What our data shows is those sites are leaking and those sites are a chemical cocktail. Whether it's the PCBs alone is up for debate.

"PCBs are suspected carcinogens, so we think they can cause cancer."

The data he found stunned him after having met people who had been worried about PCB levels near their family home for more than 30 years, saying he found levels that were "pretty much the highest I've ever seen in anything we've tested".

He added: "It's made me feel quite uncomfortable about some of those sites and what could have happened to all of those people's friends and loved ones.

"The polluter just keeps getting away with stuff left, right and centre."

These chemicals are hard to clear up, but not impossible.

Ralph Davies, who has been in the chemical remediation industry for about 35 years, said he proposed a way of cleaning up the acid tar lake in Llwyneinion near Ruabon in 2007, but never heard back from Wrexham council.

He said was "amazed" how close it was to people's homes when he visited nearly 20 years ago.

"People are still saying it does not meet the threshold for remediation, that both angers me and saddens me," he added.

"The fact it is still there, untouched, is mind blowing."

A report by an environmental engineering consultancy in 2006, seen by BBC Wales, shows that the acid tar lagoon - one of the sites in the documentary - was known to be contaminated as early as 1979.

Among the known contaminants dumped at the site is 93,100 tonnes of acid sludge from Burmah Castrol and barrels of unknown substances suspected to be from Monsanto, the report said.

Over the next 27 years, there were 18 investigations, two remediation proposals and five treatment trials but, as of 2026, the acid tar lagoon remains.

The report identified 105 possible ways contamination from the site could affect people, wildlife, property or water supplies.

This included three uncapped mine shafts beneath the lagoon that were suggested as potential pathways for contaminant movement.

In the 1980s, Clwyd County Council bought the site and legally agreed to protect the previous owner from any past, present or future claims, costs or liabilities arising from the "escape or nuisance of noxious wastes".

BP, which is responsible for Burmah Castrol, said it had no comment to make.

Emeritus professor Sue Jordan, a researcher at Swansea University, said further monitoring and investigation was needed.

After reading the BBC article about the documentary , she said she and her colleagues thought it was "an eye-opener" and it made them think "maybe there is something in this pollution".

She added that researchers still did not fully understand why some health outcomes, including congenital anomalies and stillbirths, appear higher in Wales than in parts of the UK, and believes further research is needed.

"I would very much like the minister to turn around and say Public Health Wales will look at this," she said.

"We don't want anything brushed under the carpet."

John Browne, a lawyer specialising in industrial disease claims at Slater and Gordon, said cases involving historical contamination were difficult to investigate - but not impossible.

"Time passing makes cases more difficult to prove," he said.

"Witnesses' memories fade and locating [eye]witnesses becomes increasingly challenging and difficult."

However, he said scientific, medical and forensic evidence could help establish what happened and whether exposure to hazardous substances contributed to illness.

The key question is not simply what the law was at the time, but what was known about the risks, he said, adding: "Communities affected by contamination deserve transparency and clear answers."

Public Health Wales said its Welsh cancer intelligence and surveillance unit had collected and analysed "every single case of cancer" since the 1970s.

It added: "Based on the evidence currently available, there is no indication that historical environmental pollution is responsible for an increased risk of cancer, or any other disease or illness, in these areas."

Natural Resources Wales said the Environment Agency, its predecessor, investigated the acid tar lake in 2006 and 2008 but tests concluded it did not meet the legal definition of contaminated land.

"Therefore, responsibility for the site returned and remains with Wrexham County Council as regulator."

Wrexham council said, since these investigations 20 years ago, ongoing monitoring had not identified any significant changes and there was no statutory requirement for remediation.

The Welsh government said addressing contaminated land was one of its key priorities.

"A survey of local authorities carried out by Natural Resources Wales in 2015 identified more than 9,000 potential sites requiring further investigation.

"While not all of these sites will pose a risk to human health or the environment, this figure demonstrates the scale of the issue facing regulators in Wales.

"We now intend to develop a Wales-wide strategy to progressively restore post-industrial land, so that communities are no longer exposed to potential risks."

The UK government referred the BBC to the Welsh government when asked to comment.

Constance, 61, said working for Monsanto was "absolutely dreadful".

Looking back, he said it was "quite evident that nobody was fully appraised of the potential hazard that they were exposed to".

The material was already buried when Constance arrived and it was his job to dig a 6m-deep trench around the outside of the mound before it was sealed using plastic membrane sheets and liquid clay.

While he believes this prevented airborne contamination, he is unsure if it would have stopped contamination into the Earth due to the high water table linked to the tides.

When asked if he felt safe, he said: "In terms of what we knew was there and what we were potentially exposed to, no."

Constance is in remission from cancer after having follicular lymphoma , external .

"I'm not suggesting in any way at all that it's linked, but the thought did cross my mind," he said.

In the documentary, journalists Dan Ashby and Lucy Taylor reveal a memo from Monsanto dated to 1972 which found that it knew PCBs were a danger to human health and was closing its site in the US as a result of legal action from a town.

However, it then increased its work at the plant in Newport.

"The government in the UK told the industry 'we're not going to put any restrictions on importing PCBs'," said Ashby.

"So they begin importing from around the world, hundreds of tonnes of PCBs."

Dr Megson, a reader in chemistry and environmental forensics at Manchester Metropolitan University, led the scientific data collection in the documentary.

He said: "The country is in a really dire place.

"Public pressure is the only thing that's going to make this action happen. This is our only chance, if I'm being brutally honest.

"What our data shows is those sites are leaking and those sites are a chemical cocktail. Whether it's the PCBs alone is up for debate.

"PCBs are suspected carcinogens, so we think they can cause cancer."

The data he found stunned him after having met people who had been worried about PCB levels near their family home for more than 30 years, saying he found levels that were "pretty much the highest I've ever seen in anything we've tested".

He added: "It's made me feel quite uncomfortable about some of those sites and what could have happened to all of those people's friends and loved ones.

"The polluter just keeps getting away with stuff left, right and centre."

These chemicals are hard to clear up, but not impossible.

Ralph Davies, who has been in the chemical remediation industry for about 35 years, said he proposed a way of cleaning up the acid tar lake in Llwyneinion near Ruabon in 2007, but never heard back from Wrexham council.

He said was "amazed" how close it was to people's homes when he visited nearly 20 years ago.

"People are still saying it does not meet the threshold for remediation, that both angers me and saddens me," he added.

"The fact it is still there, untouched, is mind blowing."

A report by an environmental engineering consultancy in 2006, seen by BBC Wales, shows that the acid tar lagoon - one of the sites in the documentary - was known to be contaminated as early as 1979.

Among the known contaminants dumped at the site is 93,100 tonnes of acid sludge from Burmah Castrol and barrels of unknown substances suspected to be from Monsanto, the report said.

Over the next 27 years, there were 18 investigations, two remediation proposals and five treatment trials but, as of 2026, the acid tar lagoon remains.

The report identified 105 possible ways contamination from the site could affect people, wildlife, property or water supplies.

This included three uncapped mine shafts beneath the lagoon that were suggested as potential pathways for contaminant movement.

In the 1980s, Clwyd County Council bought the site and legally agreed to protect the previous owner from any past, present or future claims, costs or liabilities arising from the "escape or nuisance of noxious wastes".

BP, which is responsible for Burmah Castrol, said it had no comment to make.

Emeritus professor Sue Jordan, a researcher at Swansea University, said further monitoring and investigation was needed.

After reading the BBC article about the documentary , she said she and her colleagues thought it was "an eye-opener" and it made them think "maybe there is something in this pollution".

She added that researchers still did not fully understand why some health outcomes, including congenital anomalies and stillbirths, appear higher in Wales than in parts of the UK, and believes further research is needed.

"I would very much like the minister to turn around and say Public Health Wales will look at this," she said.

"We don't want anything brushed under the carpet."

John Browne, a lawyer specialising in industrial disease claims at Slater and Gordon, said cases involving historical contamination were difficult to investigate - but not impossible.

"Time passing makes cases more difficult to prove," he said.

"Witnesses' memories fade and locating [eye]witnesses becomes increasingly challenging and difficult."

However, he said scientific, medical and forensic evidence could help establish what happened and whether exposure to hazardous substances contributed to illness.

The key question is not simply what the law was at the time, but what was known about the risks, he said, adding: "Communities affected by contamination deserve transparency and clear answers."

Public Health Wales said its Welsh cancer intelligence and surveillance unit had collected and analysed "every single case of cancer" since the 1970s.

It added: "Based on the evidence currently available, there is no indication that historical environmental pollution is responsible for an increased risk of cancer, or any other disease or illness, in these areas."

Natural Resources Wales said the Environment Agency, its predecessor, investigated the acid tar lake in 2006 and 2008 but tests concluded it did not meet the legal definition of contaminated land.

"Therefore, responsibility for the site returned and remains with Wrexham County Council as regulator."

Wrexham council said, since these investigations 20 years ago, ongoing monitoring had not identified any significant changes and there was no statutory requirement for remediation.

The Welsh government said addressing contaminated land was one of its key priorities.

"A survey of local authorities carried out by Natural Resources Wales in 2015 identified more than 9,000 potential sites requiring further investigation.

"While not all of these sites will pose a risk to human health or the environment, this figure demonstrates the scale of the issue facing regulators in Wales.

"We now intend to develop a Wales-wide strategy to progressively restore post-industrial land, so that communities are no longer exposed to potential risks."

The UK government referred the BBC to the Welsh government when asked to comment.

articles.title: Kurdish-led Syrian Democratic Forces group says it has dissolved after merging with the Syrian army
articles.summary: DAMASCUS, Syria — The commander of the Kurdish-led Syrian Democratic Forces on Tuesday announced the official dissolution of the group, which once controlled a de facto autonomous zone in Syria’s northeast.
articles.body: DAMASCUS, Syria — The commander of the Kurdish-led Syrian Democratic Forces on Tuesday announced the official dissolution of the group, which once controlled a de facto autonomous zone in Syria’s northeast. Speaking during a news conference at the presidential palace in Damascus, Mazloum Abdi said the SDF has completed a merger with the Syrian army and would cease to operate as an independent force. The Kurdish-led force lost most of its territory in northeast Syria to a government offensive in January and then signed the deal to merge with the army. The SDF was once the main partner of the United States in Syria as it battled the Islamic State group. But after the ouster of former Syrian President Bashar Assad in December 2024, Washington formed close ties with the new government in Damascus led by interim Syrian President Ahmad al-Sharaa, the former leader of an Islamist insurgent group. The SDF “carried a heavy responsibility during one of the most difficult periods in Syria’s history,” Abdi said. “Today, circumstances have changed, and the country has entered a new phase, one of peace and participation in building a new Syria,” he said, announcing the “end of the SDF’s mission” and “its dissolution as an independent military force.” Under the 50-year rule of the Assad dynasty in Syria, Kurds were marginalized, with many denied citizenship. Public celebrations of the Nowruz holiday — an ancient Persian springtime new year festival that is also celebrated by Kurds in Syria, Turkey and Iraq as well as Iran — were banned. Shortly after the uprising against the Assad government began in 2011, the Kurds filled the vacuum created by the withdrawal of government forces from wide areas of Syria’s northeast. The SDF at one point controlled about 25% of Syria. The Kurds were initially circumspect about the new post-Assad government and unwilling to give up their de facto autonomy. Some of the insurgent groups that took part in the offensive that ousted Assad were Turkish-backed forces that had clashed with the SDF in the past. Turkey considered the SDF to be a terrorist organization because of its ties to the Kurdistan Workers’ Party, or PKK, a separatist group that staged a decades-long insurgency in Turkey. A peace process is now underway. Kurds questioned whether the new Sunni Arab-led authorities would give them true representation in the new government, while al-Sharaa tried to woo them. During ceasefire negotiations with the SDF in January, he issued a decree strengthening Kurdish rights. It made Kurdish an official language along with Arabic, and adopted Nowruz as a national holiday. It also restored the citizenship of tens of thousands of Kurds in northeastern Hassakeh province after they were stripped of it during the 1962 census. Abdi said that al-Sharaa had promised that Kurds would have the right to education in their own language, an important issue for the country’s Kurdish population. Questions remain, including the fate of the SDF’s all-female fighting units — a sensitive point in the integration talks as many of the Damascus leaders come from a conservative background and are opposed to women in combat. But the success of the integration agreement with the SDF is a major boost to al-Sharaa’s government, which has struggled to unify the country as it begins to recover from a nearly 14-year civil war. Most of the country is now under the control of the central government in Damascus. The exception is southern Syria’s Sweida province, which is now controlled by Druze factions that are hostile to Damascus after clashes last year in which government-affiliated fighters launched sectarian revenge attacks on Druze civilians. The Druze factions have received support from Israel, which is also occupying a strip of land in southern Syria near the border with the Israeli-annexed Golan Heights.

articles.title: Muere Dolly Parton: la fabulosa vida de una de las estrellas más queridas en imágenes
articles.summary: La cantante estrella de la música country, que surgió de orígenes humildes, llegó a convertirse en una de las artistas más queridas del mundo.
articles.body:
Dolly Parton, la superestrella de la música country originaria de las Grandes Montañas Humeantes de Tennessee, pasó de unos orígenes humildes a convertirse en una de las artistas más queridas del mundo.

Esta admiración global se reflejó este martes en la cantidad de mensajes y muestras de cariño que se produjeron tras conocerse la noticia de su muerte, a los 80 años.

A lo largo de una carrera que abarcó más de 60 años, vendió más de 100 millones de discos, escribió más de 3.000 canciones y ganó 11 premios Grammy, incluido un reconocimiento a la trayectoria artística.

Siempre se describió a sí misma, ante todo, como compositora. "Es mi forma de expresarme. Es mi terapia", dijo en una ocasión.

Dolly Rebecca Parton creció en la pobreza en una cabaña de una sola habitación a orillas del río Little Pigeon, en las montañas Smoky de Tennessee, siendo la cuarta de 12 hijos.

De niña, actuó en la radio y la televisión locales, y grabó su primer sencillo a los 13 años.

Tras mudarse a Nashville al día siguiente de graduarse en la escuela secundaria del condado de Sevier, Dolly Parton consiguió su primer éxito en solitario con Dumb Blonde en 1966.

En 1967, la estrella de la música country Porter Wagoner invitó a Parton a unirse a The Porter Wagoner Show , dándole un papel fijo en su programa de televisión de distribución nacional, así como un lugar en su espectáculo teatral itinerante.

Su gran éxito llegó con el álbum Hello, I'm Dolly .

El 4 de enero de 1969 se convirtió en miembro del Grand Ole Opry , el programa radiofónico de música country más antiguo de Estados Unidos.

Parton lo describió como la "iglesia de mi corazón" y dijo que participar en él era un sueño de toda la vida.

En una memorable sesión de composición en 1973, Parton escribió dos de sus mayores éxitos: Jolene y I Will Always Love You .

Tras haber escrito miles de canciones a lo largo de su dilatada carrera, Parton afirmó que componer canciones era su mayor forma de autoexpresión.

Conocida por su imagen extravagante y deslumbrante, Dolly Parton combinó lentejuelas, ingenio y encanto para mantener una carrera que abarcó desde la música country hasta el pop comercial.

Fue cabeza de cartel en festivales y se convirtió en una estrella mundial con álbumes como Here You Come Again .

Parton también se hizo famosa por colaboraciones memorables, en particular con Kenny Rogers, cuyo dúo Islands in the Stream se convirtió en uno de los éxitos más representativos de la década de 1980.

Si bien Dolly Parton es más conocida por su extensa carrera musical, su trabajo como actriz también ha dejado una huella imborrable en el público cinematográfico.

El papel que lanzó a la fama a Parton en la pantalla grande llegó en la comedia de oficina de 1980 9 to 5 , donde compartió cartel con Jane Fonda, Lily Tomlin y Dabney Coleman.

Su interpretación de Doralee Rhodes combinó un gran sentido del humor con calidez, lo que ayudó a redefinir las expectativas sobre los artistas que dan el salto de la música al cine.

Posteriormente participó en películas como The Best Little Whorehouse in Texas , junto a Burt Reynolds, y Steel Magnolias ("Magnolias de acero").

Esta última cuenta con un reparto monumental que incluye a Julia Roberts y Sally Field junto a Shirley MacLaine, Olympia Dukakis y Daryl Hannah.

En estas interpretaciones, Parton demostró un equilibrio entre humor y profundidad emocional, a menudo dotando a las escenas de una presencia discreta y marcada.

En 1986, Dolly Parton inauguró Dollywood, un parque temático en Pigeon Forge, Tennessee, cerca de su lugar de nacimiento.

Se convirtió en una importante atracción turística, uno de los parques temáticos regionales más visitados de EE.UU..

El éxito del parque ayudó a financiar la fundación benéfica de Parton y su programa de alfabetización.

A través de su Biblioteca de la Imaginación, fundada en honor a su padre, que no sabía leer, Dolly Parton regaló más de 100 millones de libros a niños de todo el mundo.

Su propio libro, Coat of Many Colours , fue el libro número 100 millones que ese programa donó a la colección de la Biblioteca del Congreso de Estados Unidos.

Un ayuntamiento de Escocia anunció que dedicaría un día al año a Dolly Parton para conmemorar el impacto de su programa de fomento de la lectura.

Parton donó personalmente millones a la investigación médica y al socorro en casos de desastre.

La cantante también lideró varias iniciativas importantes de ayuda en casos de desastre, entre las que destaca la creación de My People Fund tras los incendios forestales de las Grandes Montañas Humeantes de 2016, que distribuyó unos US$10 millones a las familias que perdieron sus hogares.

Reunió a un elenco estelar de artistas para un teletón de tres horas con el fin de recaudar fondos.

En 2024, prometió US$2 millones para ayudar a los damnificados por el huracán Helene en el este de Tennessee y los Apalaches, combinando una donación personal con el apoyo equivalente de sus empresas y su fundación.

La actuación de Parton en el Festival de Glastonbury de 2014 se convirtió rápidamente en una de las actuaciones más emblemáticas en la sección de "Leyendas" de la historia del evento.

Con una de las mayores afluencias diurnas que ha tenido el festival, estimada en más de 180.000 personas, convirtió el escenario Pyramid en un coro multitudinario, con interpretaciones de Jolene , 9 to 5 y I Will Always Love You que provocaron escenas de participación casi unánime del público.

En 2019, Parton celebró sus 50 años como miembro del Opry con un importante programa especial de televisión titulado Dolly Parton: 50 Years at the Opry .

El evento incluyó actuaciones y homenajes de otros artistas de música country.

Su relación de décadas con el Opry ayudó a consolidar su estatus como guardián de la tradición de la música country y como escenario para las estrellas modernas.

Parton comenzó a alejarse gradualmente de las grandes giras, diciendo que ya no quería pasar largos periodos de tiempo en la carretera.

En cambio, se centró en conciertos selectos, nuevos proyectos discográficos y apariciones en pantalla, incluyendo Dolly Parton's Heartstrings , Mountain Magic y Christmas on the Square para Netflix .

En 2021, Parton recibió públicamente la vacuna contra la covid-19 en el Centro Médico de la Universidad de Vanderbilt, aprovechando la ocasión para animar a otros a hacer lo mismo.

Interpretó una versión adaptada de su éxito Jolene , cantando: "Vacuna, vacuna, vacuna, vacuna, te lo ruego, por favor no lo dudes".

La incorporación de Parton al Salón de la Fama del Rock and Roll en 2022 marcó un giro de autoconciencia muy característico de ella.

Tras haber dicho inicialmente que no se había "ganado" el honor, más tarde lo aceptó con humor, declarando "ahora soy una estrella del rock", antes de interpretar su nueva canción Rockin' , escrita especialmente para la ceremonia, un paso simbólico hacia su posterior álbum de rock Rockstar.

En 2023, Parton protagonizó otro momento memorable en directo cuando actuó en el espectáculo del medio tiempo del partido de Acción de Gracias de los Dallas Cowboys, luciendo un traje de animadora del equipo adornado con pedrería.

Más recientemente, Parton continuó compaginando las pérdidas personales con nuevos proyectos creativos.

Después del fallecimiento de su marido, Carl Dean, en 2025, lanzó If You Hadn't Been There en su homenaje, al tiempo que continuaba con el desarrollo de Dolly: A True Original Musical , la producción teatral basada en su vida y carrera.

A principios de 2026, Parton pronunció un discurso de homenaje pregrabado para Ozzy Osbourne en los premios BRIT en Manchester, donde Ozzy recibió un premio póstumo a la trayectoria artística.

Su discurso fue breve, pero constituyó uno de los momentos más emotivos de la ceremonia.

Parton tenía previsto regresar a los escenarios para una breve temporada en Las Vegas, pero este mes anunció que cancelaba la serie de conciertos debido a problemas de salud, y les dijo a sus fans que necesitaba "un poco más de tiempo para recuperarse".

Ella seguirá siendo un ícono cultural recordado por su generosidad y humor, así como por su extraordinaria capacidad para componer canciones, el arte que constituye la base de un catálogo que ha dado forma a la música country moderna y ha trascendido generaciones.

articles.title: Female Virginia officer sues police department after allegedly sharing locker room with biological male
articles.summary: Former Norfolk police officer Meghan Grabow sued her police department earlier this month after sharing a women's changing room with a biological male in 202...
articles.body:
A former Norfolk, Virginia , police officer filed a lawsuit against the city and its police chief earlier this month after the police department allegedly allowed a biological male to use the women's locker rooms.

According to the documents obtained by Fox News Digital , the Aug. 10 legal complaint stemmed from an August 2024 incident in which former Norfolk police officer Meghan Grabow was changing in the women's locker room and stripped down to her underwear when a recruit described as a "biological male who identifies as a woman" entered the room wearing a suit and tie. Grabow said that the recruit looked at her "as a man would look at a woman" before moving to another part of the locker room.

Grabow claimed that when she spoke to her superiors about her discomfort, she was told to "learn to deal with it" and "find another locker room" if she was uncomfortable.

San Francisco Ymca Changes Locker Room Rules After Transgender Controversy: Report

In addition to this incident, Grabow said that she and other concerned officers were told by police chief Mark Talbot that the "woman" hired by the department "will use the restroom that's appropriate for her gender" and were repeatedly instructed to refer to the recruit as "she."

Other officers also voiced concerns that they were not warned about sharing facilities with a biological male , something Talbot acknowledged could have been handled "better."

Appeals Court Revives Lawsuit By Alaska Airlines Flight Attendants Fired After Opposing Pride Message

Grabow later received an indefinite suspension pending termination in 2025 over a minor traffic violation committed prior to the incident after attempting to voice a complaint. Other officers have since left the department over their backlash to the transgender policy, the complaint states.

Grabow is seeking $15 million in compensatory damages, claiming Talbot and the police department were guilty of intentional infliction of emotional distress as well as violating her religious freedoms by forcing her to share a changing facility with a biological male and validate transgender ideology against her Catholic beliefs .

Christian Lifeguard Who Refused Pride Flag Duties And Was Suspended Is Now Headed Toward Trial

Attorney Scott Lloyd, who is representing Grabow in the case, told Fox News Digital in a statement that they are determined to protect female-only spaces through this case.

"We need to defend private spaces for the women who rely on them. Officer Grabow has done a brave and admirable thing by stepping forward, but it shouldn't have come to this," Lloyd said.

The Norfolk Police Department declined to comment to Fox News Digital, saying that it "cannot comment on pending litigation or personnel-related matters."

Under 2020 guidelines for the Norfolk Police Department, employees are encouraged not to question a transgender person's identity except for "articulable reasons," such as if they are related to a crime.

"Employees will respect an individual's gender identity and gender expression. An individual's gender expression may be traits that are not typically associated with a person's assigned sex at birth; these expressions may include wigs, prosthetics, makeup, adopted name, tone of voice, clothing, mannerisms, etc.," the 2020 general order read.

articles.title: Lindsay Clancy's Last Words to Her 3 Kids Before Their Deaths Revealed
articles.summary: Lindsay Clancy’s last words to her and husband Patrick Clancy's three kids before their 2023 deaths were revealed as Dr. Kirk Heilbrun testified in the trial...
articles.body:
Content warning: This story discusses violence against children and suicidal ideation.

New details are coming to light in the Lindsay Clancy case.

During court proceedings for the 36-year-old—who is on trial for three counts of first-degree murder after admitting to killing her and then-husband Patrick Clancy 's kids Cora , 5, Dawson , 3 and Callan , 8 months, in 2023—forensic psychologist Dr. Kirk Heilbrun revealed the last words that the former labor and delivery nurse told her children before strangling them and trying to kill herself.

During his testimony Aug. 24, which was livestreamed by Associated Press , Heilbrun—who evaluated Lindsay for three days in April—testified that she killed her children as part of what he described as "altruistic filicide," saying she believed they would suffer without her and that killing them would allow them to be "together in heaven."

As she killed them, she told the children, according to Heilbrun, "Go to God, baby. Go to God."

The psychologist also revealed what Lindsay said to Patrick after he returned home and asked what she had done. According to Heilbrun, she replied, "I tried to kill myself."

Dolly Parton, Country Music Legend, Dead at 80

Dolly Parton Shared How She Wanted to Be Remembered Before Death

Lindsay admitted to strangling her three children to death using an exercise band in January 2023 before attempting to take her own life by jumping out of a second-story window. She suffered a fall that left her paralyzed from the waist down.

While she has not denied killing her three kids, Lindsay has pleaded not guilty for criminal responsibility in their murders due to her state of mind during the incident, which her defense attorney Kevin Reddington is arguing was compromised due to postpartum psychosis.

Heilbrun said Lindsay's response to Patrick was inconsistent with psychosis, noting that someone experiencing hallucinations likely would have replied differently.

However, he also noted that Lindsay shared with him that she did hear a male voice about 18 minutes before the murders, which said, "Kill the kids so you can kill yourself."

"The way she described this as happening is that she heard a voice that she'd never heard before, experienced a hallucination and she's never experienced it since. But she only experienced it for the 18 minutes or so that it took to kill the children," Heilbrun testified. "To put it mildly, that would be a very, very unusual pattern or manifestation of how this kind of thing comes about. Very unusual."

Heilbrun told the court he diagnosed Lindsay with Bipolar II disorder. Saying she experienced both manic and depressive episodes, he admitted the diagnosis was difficult to reach "because of all the diagnoses in the records and all the symptoms that she experienced."

Heilbrun also brought up Lindsay's Catholic faith, which prompted Reddington to request a mistrial. Judge William Sullivan denied the motion.

Lindsay Clancy 's now-ex-husband was the first witness called to testify during her murder trial, which began July 27 in Plymouth Superior Court. The 35-year-old former nurse has not denied killing daughter Cora , 5, and sons Dawson , 3, and Callan , 8 months, but has pleaded not guilty of murder, the defense attributing her actions to postpartum psychosis. Patrick Clancy testified that Lindsay struggled with her mental health after giving birth to Callan in May 2023, according to CNN . She also sought treatment after Dawson was born in 2019, he said, "but it didn't last very long." Lindsay's "big spiral," as he referred to it, occurred in December 2023 after she started taking a new medication, one of several she'd been prescribed since September, Patrick said. He testified that Lindsay told him she had "intrusive thoughts" about harming their children and herself. He didn't worry about the kids' safety, he said, because she didn't seem to have "any intention" of actually hurting them. On Dec. 31, Patrick said, Lindsay went to the E.R. at Massachusetts General Hospital "because she was still talking about thoughts of suicide . She was admitted to an affiliated psychiatric facility, and when she was discharged Jan. 5 she seemed "much better."

On Jan. 24, 2023, Lindsay "was having one of her best days," Patrick testified, per CNN , recalling that his then-wife built a snowman in the yard. "She was playing with the kids," he said, "and she seemed in a good mood." That morning she had taken Cora to a doctor's appointment and he had texted her a picture of Dawson after he "dressed himself completely for the first time." Patrick told the court he had felt "hopeful" since his wife's release from the hospital. "Her mood seemed better," he said. "She was more active, and she was able...to partake in more things." Before he left to pick up dinner and medication for Cora, he said he kissed one of the kids on the head and told them he'd "be right back." Prosecutors allege Lindsay sent Patrick on errands to get him out of the house on purpose. Then, Plymouth County Assistant District Attorney Shanan Buckingham said in her opening statement, she strangled the children with exercise bands "deliberately and meticulously." Patrick testified July 29 that no one told him he shouldn't leave Linday alone with their kids, telling the court, "I didn't know what psychosis was until after this happened."

In the audio recording of Patrick's seven-minute 911 call that was played in court July 29, according to the Associated Press , he's heard telling the dispatcher, who repeatedly asks what happened, "She killed the kids!"

Lindsay wrote about her struggles, including that she felt "incredibly sad and guilty" about not breastfeeding Callan, according to journal excerpts read to jurors Aug. 5. "I want help," she wrote in an entry read by her attorney. "I want to be well." In another, she said, "I have crazy brain fog. I feel like I can't make a plan. I live moment to moment waiting for the next nap time. I'm terrified of Cal getting overtired now because I feel can't help him."

When Lindsay was hospitalized after killing her children and allegedly tried to take her own life, she tested positive for the antidepressant mirtazapine, the mood stabilizer lamotrigine, the antidepressant trazodone and quetiapine, a drug used to treat schizophrenia, bipolar disorder and severe depression, forensic toxicologist Justin Brower testified Aug. 5. He said, per The Guardian , that his lab found that only the level of quetiapine in her blood was slightly elevated, but it wasn't at a "toxic" or "suicidal concentration." He further described the levels in her blood as "not consistent" with someone who takes a bunch of pills before trying to end her life. Under defense cross-examination, Brower also said that toxicology results "don't tell the entire story." Lindsay's attorney Kevin Reddington said in his July 28 opening statement that she has bipolar disorder and medication worsened her condition. On the day she killed Cora, Dawson and Callan, Reddington said, she heard a voice telling her, "'This is your last chance. Kill the children so you can kill yourself.'"

The Clancy family's nanny Elaine Rossi testified Aug. 5 that she had no concerns about Lindsay's fitness as a mother. "I observed a wonderful mom who loved her kids," Rossi said. "She was concerned about their safety, and Callan eating and sleeping. She was a wonderful mother."

Andrea Hennigan , who previously worked with the defendant at Massachusetts General, testified Aug. 6 that Lindsay told her at lunch after Callan was born that she didn't plan to go back to work as a labor-and-delivery nurse because she "was not in a mental state to take care of patients." "She talked about insomnia and not feeling herself," Hennigan said, per the AP . "I believe she might have used the words brain fog or something like that." Lindsay texted her in January 2023, Hennigan said, that she was experiencing "bad or negative side effects" from medication.

articles.body: For Heather Porter, graduation day in Phoenix was not simply the end of a university course. It marked the close of several demanding years in which studying had to fit around a large family, foster care and a sudden change in the way she experienced the world.As reported by People, Porter received her masterâs degree from Grand Canyon University on April 29, 2026, walking across the commencement stage in a purple gown. Among those watching was her seven-year-old daughter, Rebekah, who reached across the aisle to hold her motherâs hand during the ceremony.By then, Porter had already spent years adjusting to significant hearing loss and the complications that followed. She had also continued raising her children while completing her graduate studies online.When hearing loss began to change Porterâs everyday lifePorter first noticed that something was wrong with her hearing while she was still an undergraduate. Conversations became harder to follow, and information that seemed straightforward to others could leave her struggling to keep up.As reported, the problem was eventually traced to an autoimmune condition affecting her inner ear. Her diagnosis came during the COVID-19 pandemic, a period when Porter was already dealing with the uncertainty of her changing hearing.The effect was not limited to classrooms or conversations. Porter described feeling increasingly cut off from people around her, including members of her own family. There was a period of grief as she adjusted to the possibility that her hearing would not return to what it had been.âI was struggling to understand things that other people understood easily,â she said of watching other peopleâs lips, as reported by Grand Canyon University News.Her cochlear implant opened a new door to sound, but complications followedPorter eventually received financial assistance that allowed her to have a cochlear implant. The device gave her another way to access sound, but her experience with it was far from straightforward.About a year and a half after the implant was fitted, it began malfunctioning. Porter experienced pain and other problems, and medical examinations showed that the device was failing. She was eventually told that electricity was leaking from the implant into her head. Surgery was required to replace it.The second implant became part of the routine she gradually built around her hearing. Porter also uses sign language, something that became particularly meaningful as she became more connected with the deaf and hard-of-hearing community.She has described learning sign language as an unexpected gift during a period when much of her life had been changing.Graduate school happened alongside raising 11 childrenPorter's university work was only one part of her life. She was raising a family of 11 children while completing her degree, including children who had joined the family through foster care and adoption.Her experience with foster care began when she and her then-husband took in a child and later decided to foster that child's three older siblings as well. Porter was 25 at the time.She later recalled that she did not want the siblings to be separated from one another, so the family took all four children in. Porter ultimately gave birth to six of her children. Her youngest, the 11th, was adopted while she was already in graduate school.That meant coursework and family responsibilities were running side by side. There were days when the demands of the degree felt difficult to manage, Porter acknowledged, and she has spoken about the tears that came during the programme. Still, she kept going.Her graduation marked more than a degree after years of challengesThe commencement ceremony gave Porter a chance to mark the achievement with some of the people who had been part of the years it took to reach it.Images from the ceremony show her daughter Rebekah reaching towards her across the aisle, while another photograph captures Porter receiving her degree. Her sister, Annie Pearce, was also there and later embraced her after the ceremony. Pearce said Porter's familiarity with sign language and her existing connection with the deaf community had become an important part of how she handled the loss of her hearing.For Porter, the significance of the degree extends beyond having another qualification. She now hopes to use what she has learned in work with people who are hard of hearing.Turning her own struggle into hope for othersPorter plans to pursue work as a psychotherapist, with a particular interest in serving the hard-of-hearing community. Her own experience with hearing loss has given her a perspective that she hopes will be useful when working with people facing similar difficulties.She is also considering what could come after the masterâs degree. A Ph.D. remains a possibility, as does teaching internationally. She summed up what she had taken from those years in a message about facing difficult circumstances without allowing them to define the rest of a person's life.âThere is hope, no matter how low life feels,â Porter said.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: Brazil fines TikTok $30m for child data privacy violations
articles.summary: Owner ByteDance ordered to erase illegally obtained child data in Brazil as crackdown on tech giants intensifies.
articles.body:
Brazil's data protection authority has fined TikTok's parent company, ByteDance, nearly $30m for the alleged mishandling of children and teenagers' personal data, in the nation's latest move against social media companies.

The regulatory body said in its ruling that TikTok had breached data privacy laws across both logged-in accounts and guest browsing sessions by collecting and processing young users' personal information without a valid legal basis or adequate safeguards.

The regulator estimated that TikTok may have processed the data of at least 8 million children, highlighting what they said were systemic deficiencies within the platform's age-verification mechanism.

The company can still appeal the decision in the next 10 days, according to the regulator.

The ruling also includes an order for TikTok to erase all data amassed illegally.

Brazil's regulatory authority also mandated the company to formulate an improved comprehensive youth-protection framework, stressing that TikTok's "logged-out feed", which allows users to browse content without creating an account, enables widespread use ‌of the ⁠platform by minors while bypassing age-verification checks.

According to the regulator, the feature is available in Brazil but not in the United States or Europe, where access is solely restricted to registered users.

Earlier this month, the regulator ordered the social media platform Discord to suspend its livestreaming feature across the country, accusing the platform of failing to protect children and teenagers. The move came after a 13-year-old girl died by suicide following a livestream in which authorities say she was encouraged to harm herself.

The voice and text chat app, hugely popular with gamers, launched in 2015.

Brazil's government, under President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, and the Supreme Court have tried to regulate internet use by minors, with mixed results so far, at a moment when countries such as Australia, Canada and Indonesia are undertaking similar efforts.

articles.title: Calls for GPS monitoring of domestic abuse suspects after murder of Stacy Hunter
articles.summary: An online petition calls for greater use of technology to protect women from abusive partners following the killing of Stacy Hunter in Renfrewshire.
articles.body:
Domestic abuse campaigners are calling for greater use of location tracking technology to monitor high-risk suspects following the murder of a woman in Renfrewshire last month.

An online petition is calling for a "Stacy's law" in memory of Stacy Hunter who was killed at her home near Houston by her estranged husband while he was on bail.

Scottish ministers have previously faced criticism over the slow rollout of Global Positioning System (GPS) equipment, which is used far less in Scotland than in some other countries.

The Scottish government said it was listening to victims and support organisations and would carefully consider the petition.

Woman found dead was murdered, police say, as man's death still 'unexplained'

Man found dead with murdered wife had been accused of attacking her

The campaign has been started by Lynne Mackenzie, herself a domestic abuse survivor, who lives a few miles from the isolated cottage where Stacy was killed in July.

Stacy's husband Jim Mair, 43, whose body was found beside her, had been charged with assaulting her but had reportedly been granted bail on condition that he did not approach her.

While Mackenzie did not know Stacy personally, she said she was shocked at her murder which happened just six days after the death of another domestic abuse victim, Vikki Soloman, in Edinburgh.

She told BBC Scotland News the killings led her to question whether enough was being done to protect women in Stacy's situation.

"Every time driving in and out of the village I was aware of the police at the end of the road," she said.

"And it really got me thinking what could we have done? What could have been put in place beforehand? What else do we need?"

She has been in contact with Stacy's family who have agreed for her name to be associated with the campaign.

The petition calls for high-risk domestic abuse perpetrators or suspects released on bail to have their location monitored using GPS equipment.

This could include individually assessed exclusion zones around victim's homes or workplaces and alerts that trigger police responses when conditions are breached.

Mike Nellis, emeritus professor of criminal and community justice at the University of Strathclyde and one of the UK's leading experts on electronic monitoring, said it was perfectly feasible to introduce such a system.

He said it could work by setting an exclusion zone around a victim's home that triggered an alert if an abuser violated it, although the zone would have to be sufficiently large to allow time for police to get there first.

Prof Nellis said that while Scotland has been slow to embrace GPS technology, the campaign could now find itself "pushing at an open door" because ministers are actively exploring ways of reducing the prison population.

However, he cautioned that no system was foolproof.

"I think probably every jurisdiction that has used it has at one point in time had an offender who still managed to assault, injure or kill the victim," he told BBC Scotland News.

"It's a helpful solution but it's not perfect."

He also added that some women's support groups have in the past voiced concern that such systems might give a false sense of security.

In Scotland, electronic tagging has mainly relied on older radio frequency (RF) equipment which is focused on home curfews or detention.

These devices are linked to a receiver in the offender's home and cannot track movements away from the property.

Last year, the independent public body Community Justice Scotland (CJS) issued an urgent National Improvement Recommendation to the Scottish government urging it to accelerate the expansion of more sophisticated monitoring systems.

CJS expressed frustration that neither GPS nor alcohol monitoring technologies had been adopted in Scotland despite an expert group having backed them in 2016.

By contrast, both technologies have already been widely used in England and Wales since 2018 and there are plans to start imposing new restriction zones on offenders this autumn.

Scotland's victims minister, Kirsten Oswald, said her thoughts were with Stacy's family.

In a statement she said: "We are listening carefully to victims and support organisations about what more can be done to prevent and tackle violence against women and girls and we will carefully consider the petition.

"The first minister has pledged his personal leadership on tackling the scourge of violence against women and girls.

"As the first minister has made clear, government has a vital role to play in tackling violence against women and girls, but lasting change requires all of us to play our part."

She added: "Men, in particular, must challenge sexism, confront abusive behaviour and help create a culture where every woman and girl can live free from violence, abuse and fear.

"While decisions on bail and remand are always a matter for the independent court, bail can be electronically monitored."

Lynne Mackenzie is a co-founder of Rise Against Abuse , a not-for-profit group which supports those affected by domestic abuse, but she has started the petition in an individual capacity.

Stacy's family now prefer her to be remembered by her pre-marriage surname Hunter, rather than her husband's name Mair.
