articles.title: Does 'rewilded' land need better wildfire prevention measures?
articles.summary: RSPB is considering measures it can take to improve resilience in the wake of a five week long fire
articles.body:
As we're driving in a pickup truck to see the aftermath of a huge fire which burnt for more than a month in the Cairngorms, I spot fresh smoke coming from the ground.

My guide - RSPB Scotland's site manager at the Abernethy nature reserve, Ben Oliver-Jones - puts the vehicle in reverse and we jump out to see what's happening.

It's one of several hot-spots which keeps emerging a full week after firefighters left the scene , which Ben likens to a game of whack-a-mole in an already charred landscape where the smell of burning still hangs heavily in the air.

But while the small pockets of smouldering vegetation are still being dealt with, attention is turning to improving wildfire protection.

More than 2,500 hectares of moorland and forest - about 10 square miles - was destroyed in the fire, which led to the evacuation of an entire village and where the smoke could be seen and smelt 60 miles (96.5km) away in Aberdeen.

Like a growing number of Scotland's estates, the Loch Garten and Abernethy nature reserve is being managed for ecological restoration - what others might describe as 'rewilding', a now polarising term which the RSPB avoids using.

Opponents have argued that the process leaves areas more vulnerable to uncontrollable fires, which the charity disputes, but it has identified significant land management changes it plans to make.

The changes focus on four key areas: fire breaks, wetlands, heather management and tree planting.

While the estate's network of tracks functioned as a fire break in some locations, in other areas strong winds helped high flames jump the gap.

Experts say fire from burning heather can reach heights of six metres and that fire breaks need to be three times the flame height.

RSPB Scotland says it now acknowledges that fire breaks need to be wider and has already started that process on its long network of forest trails.

Machines have been used to remove vegetation on either side of the track with the hope that what remains would not create such high flames if it were to ignite.

While it might look desolate now, the hope is that some insects and plant species will eventually colonise the ground either sides of the tracks.

It also plans to create more ponds and wet areas around the site which can be used as a source of water to pump onto fires.

A small fire on the reserve in June was extinguished using water from a pond created with cash from the Scottish government's nature restoration fund as a habitat for species like rare dragonflies.

The charity says it's working to raise water tables where bogs have been drained and create new areas of standing water for fire fighting.

Peatlands have proved problematic for wildfires because the fire can spread through the peat, deep underground as well as on the surface.

It's a problem for degraded peatland which makes up about 80% of Scotland's total, but for those in a near-natural state the peat can act as a defence.

In good condition, they keep the water level high, bringing moisture to the landscape.

Its effectiveness was demonstrated during a large fire near Melvich, Sutherland, in 2019 which reached an area that had been re-wetted 20 years earlier.

Roxane Anderson from the University of the Highlands and Islands (UNI) studied the land before and after the fire and says any damage to wet peatland was superficial and on the surface.

She argues that's a reason for accelerating peatland restoration which is currently targeting 400,000 hectares - about 1,500 square miles - by 2040 and describes it as "a complete no brainer."

"We should do it as much as we can, as quickly as we can and as strategically as we can, especially in the context of this changing climate."

On Monday, Scotland's chief fire officer published an open letter calling for better wildlife planning and urging a "more formal and proportionate fire safety regime" to match that for businesses in urban settings.

It comes as the Scottish government enters the final stages of introducing licences for muirburn - the controlled burning of heather on moorland primarily managed for grouse shooting.

Ministers have brought in the licences to make moorland more "environmentally sustainable", but Scottish Land and Estates say the practice is a valuable tool for reducing vegetation which can act as fuel to a wildfire.

RSPB Scotland does not practice muirburn but accepts that the "fuel load" does need to be managed.

It has been doing that through grazing cattle, which eat the vegetation, while in other areas land managers have used machines to cut and mulch the grass, gorse, bracken and heather.

While some sporting estates remain opposed to "rewilding", others have embraced some of the elements of ecological restoration.

The Rottal estate in the Angus Glens has been working with the RSPB for several years now and owner Dee Ward believes there is a lot of common ground.

He has been re-wetting peatland, planting trees and encouraging wading birds and says that while the "ideological extremists" have been holding the narrative, a lot more estates are trying to find the middle ground.

He added: "There are people that are very anti-grouse shooting. Fair enough, that's your choice. But that's clouding their view about muirburn because they're saying because grouse shooters do it, it must be bad."

Dee urges both sides to begin looking at land management practices through the lens of preventing wildfires and consider sharing appropriate methods.

The fourth move RSPB Scotland plans is the introduction of more broadleaved trees in its woodlands.

It says that while pines contain flammable resins, species such as alder, rowan, aspen and birch are higher in moisture content which means they do not burn as easily.

Abernethy hosts the largest and most important remnant of Scotland's ancient Caledonian pine forest and so the Scots pines are an important part of the mix.

But the charity wants to explore the option of increasing the proportion of other species, which would have occurred naturally in the original forest anyway.

Michael Bruce, owner of the Glen Tannar estate in Aberdeenshire, specialises in controlled burning of moorland and helps the Scottish Fire and Rescue Service with its wildfire forecasting.

He says that there hasn't been enough academic research and modelling in the UK on how wildfires behave to make land management changes meaningful.

While two significant studies have been carried out in Scotland over the past 25 years, neither has been long-term or consistent and he believes events of the summer demonstrate the need for improved understanding.

articles.title: Does 'rewilded' land need better wildfire prevention measures?
articles.summary: RSPB is considering measures it can take to improve resilience in the wake of a five week long fire
articles.body:
As we're driving in a pickup truck to see the aftermath of a huge fire which burnt for more than a month in the Cairngorms, I spot fresh smoke coming from the ground.

My guide - RSPB Scotland's site manager at the Abernethy nature reserve, Ben Oliver-Jones - puts the vehicle in reverse and we jump out to see what's happening.

It's one of several hot-spots which keeps emerging a full week after firefighters left the scene , which Ben likens to a game of whack-a-mole in an already charred landscape where the smell of burning still hangs heavily in the air.

But while the small pockets of smouldering vegetation are still being dealt with, attention is turning to improving wildfire protection.

More than 2,500 hectares of moorland and forest - about 10 square miles - was destroyed in the fire, which led to the evacuation of an entire village and where the smoke could be seen and smelt 60 miles (96.5km) away in Aberdeen.

Like a growing number of Scotland's estates, the Loch Garten and Abernethy nature reserve is being managed for ecological restoration - what others might describe as 'rewilding', a now polarising term which the RSPB avoids using.

Opponents have argued that the process leaves areas more vulnerable to uncontrollable fires, which the charity disputes, but it has identified significant land management changes it plans to make.

The changes focus on four key areas: fire breaks, wetlands, heather management and tree planting.

While the estate's network of tracks functioned as a fire break in some locations, in other areas strong winds helped high flames jump the gap.

Experts say fire from burning heather can reach heights of six metres and that fire breaks need to be three times the flame height.

RSPB Scotland says it now acknowledges that fire breaks need to be wider and has already started that process on its long network of forest trails.

Machines have been used to remove vegetation on either side of the track with the hope that what remains would not create such high flames if it were to ignite.

While it might look desolate now, the hope is that some insects and plant species will eventually colonise the ground either sides of the tracks.

It also plans to create more ponds and wet areas around the site which can be used as a source of water to pump onto fires.

A small fire on the reserve in June was extinguished using water from a pond created with cash from the Scottish government's nature restoration fund as a habitat for species like rare dragonflies.

The charity says it's working to raise water tables where bogs have been drained and create new areas of standing water for fire fighting.

Peatlands have proved problematic for wildfires because the fire can spread through the peat, deep underground as well as on the surface.

It's a problem for degraded peatland which makes up about 80% of Scotland's total, but for those in a near-natural state the peat can act as a defence.

In good condition, they keep the water level high, bringing moisture to the landscape.

Its effectiveness was demonstrated during a large fire near Melvich, Sutherland, in 2019 which reached an area that had been re-wetted 20 years earlier.

Roxane Anderson from the University of the Highlands and Islands (UNI) studied the land before and after the fire and says any damage to wet peatland was superficial and on the surface.

She argues that's a reason for accelerating peatland restoration which is currently targeting 400,000 hectares - about 1,500 square miles - by 2040 and describes it as "a complete no brainer."

"We should do it as much as we can, as quickly as we can and as strategically as we can, especially in the context of this changing climate."

On Monday, Scotland's chief fire officer published an open letter calling for better wildlife planning and urging a "more formal and proportionate fire safety regime" to match that for businesses in urban settings.

It comes as the Scottish government enters the final stages of introducing licences for muirburn - the controlled burning of heather on moorland primarily managed for grouse shooting.

Ministers have brought in the licences to make moorland more "environmentally sustainable", but Scottish Land and Estates say the practice is a valuable tool for reducing vegetation which can act as fuel to a wildfire.

RSPB Scotland does not practice muirburn but accepts that the "fuel load" does need to be managed.

It has been doing that through grazing cattle, which eat the vegetation, while in other areas land managers have used machines to cut and mulch the grass, gorse, bracken and heather.

While some sporting estates remain opposed to "rewilding", others have embraced some of the elements of ecological restoration.

The Rottal estate in the Angus Glens has been working with the RSPB for several years now and owner Dee Ward believes there is a lot of common ground.

He has been re-wetting peatland, planting trees and encouraging wading birds and says that while the "ideological extremists" have been holding the narrative, a lot more estates are trying to find the middle ground.

He added: "There are people that are very anti-grouse shooting. Fair enough, that's your choice. But that's clouding their view about muirburn because they're saying because grouse shooters do it, it must be bad."

Dee urges both sides to begin looking at land management practices through the lens of preventing wildfires and consider sharing appropriate methods.

The fourth move RSPB Scotland plans is the introduction of more broadleaved trees in its woodlands.

It says that while pines contain flammable resins, species such as alder, rowan, aspen and birch are higher in moisture content which means they do not burn as easily.

Abernethy hosts the largest and most important remnant of Scotland's ancient Caledonian pine forest and so the Scots pines are an important part of the mix.

But the charity wants to explore the option of increasing the proportion of other species, which would have occurred naturally in the original forest anyway.

Michael Bruce, owner of the Glen Tannar estate in Aberdeenshire, specialises in controlled burning of moorland and helps the Scottish Fire and Rescue Service with its wildfire forecasting.

He says that there hasn't been enough academic research and modelling in the UK on how wildfires behave to make land management changes meaningful.

While two significant studies have been carried out in Scotland over the past 25 years, neither has been long-term or consistent and he believes events of the summer demonstrate the need for improved understanding.

He believes there is no silver bullet which will prevent a wildfire starting or spreading but that estates "need to build up layers of defence".

articles.title: I was in so much pain I could barely feed my cats - now I'm back as a pro wrestler
articles.summary: The AEW star Jamie Hayter is set for two big shows in Glasgow and at Wembley Stadium in London this week.
articles.body:
Professional wrestling storylines are often built around surprise moments, from unexpected returns to sudden plot twists.

However when British star Jamie Hayter suffered two herniated discs in her back in 2023, she feared she would never get back in the ring.

It left her in constant pain, barely able to feed her cats - and wondering if her career was over.

But the grappler, who competes with All Elite Wrestling, told BBC News that the experience gave her a better perspective on her wrestling.

And the 31-year-old from Southampton is back on home turf this week, performing in two shows at Glasgow's OVO Hydro arena and then at AEW's biggest event of the year, called All In and held at Wembley Stadium on Sunday.

Her injury left her out of action for a year.

"The worst was the first few months because I was really unsure of things," she said.

"The pain was at its highest and I was bed bound – the most I could do was get up, feed my cats, make a coffee and then wobble back to bed.

"I was sitting there depressed, think I'm not doing anything, nothing is going on in my life, and it was hard to see a positive light. Weeks felt like they were taking years to go by.

"It helped me come back with a better mentality for wrestling than I had before, just more mellowed out and with a better understanding of what is worth getting upset over."

Hayter and her tag team partner, fellow Brit Alex Windsor, are in one of Sunday's featured bouts, challenging for the promotion's women's tag team titles in front of more than 40,000 people.

It comes about a decade after Hayter learned she had ADHD. She says her career of bumps and bruises is helping her cope with the diagnosis.

"It was not a surprise because my family are all neurodivergent and my siblings have autism," she recalls.

"At school someone would say 'oh, you might have ADHD' but it never went beyond that, other than getting a little extra help for exams which I always really struggled with.

"It was a relief being diagnosed at the end of the day. It meant I can understand my brain a little better, and how I process and work with things."

More stories from Glasgow & West Scotland

The wrestler, real name Paige Woodling, says she can still find things overwhelming a lot of the time.

Being in the ring, though, has proved to be a help over the years, letting her "focus on one thing".

"I need to be in the zone with it, and I wish my brain could do that with other things too. But I think it mixes a lot of things together – there's an audience I want to entertain, it's my job, there are consequences if you don't do it well and I never want to let down the people who are there."

Given Hayter is regarded as one of the top wrestlers in AEW - the world's second biggest promotion behind industry giant World Wrestling Entertainment - it might seem unlikely that she would let down people.

Away from the squared circle though, and she admits things can be harder when the spotlights are off.

"You hear people say 'oh, being neurodivergent is my super power' and I hate that, because it's a debilitating thing. It can be a lot to deal with, and at points I do slip – I'll get overwhelmed with having places to be, or things to do, and life things go out the window.

"I'm still learning to manage it all better."

Hayter first fell in love with the industry when young, watching online clips and videos of matches, with brash anti-hero Stone Cold Steve Austin - a beer drinking, brawling and swearing star of the late 90s and early 2000s - an early inspiration.

"Nothing has ever captured me like wrestling did, not movies or TV or music," she says.

"Wrestling had this weird trance on me. I wanted to watch more, understand it and eventually do it, and I decided I was going to be a wrestler or a stuntwoman."

A prolific career on the British wrestling scene followed, which led to a stint in Japan, and a blink-and-you'll -miss-it appearance on WWE's development show NXT, where she lost to Scottish wrestler Piper Niven in Glasgow.

That was one of very few Scottish appearances for Hayter, who says she's eager to sample a "proper Glasgow crowd" at the Hydro, as AEW record their flagship TV shows Dynamite and Collision in the city.

She has been with the company since 2021, becoming a fixture of their women's division and winning the women's singles title on one occasion .

Earlier this year she was paired up with Norwich native Alex Windsor to form a team calling the Brawling Birds - a fan favourite duo fond of both brawls and booze.

"It's pretty close to us in real life, " she laughs.

"We're pretty tomboyish, we don't take things too seriously and we both like going to the pub. We're loud and boisterous but in a good way, and then you crank that up to 10 – we do ham it up a bit for an American audience."

After recovering from her debilitating injury, Hayter is now in far more optimistic spirits, chatting in the bar of a Glasgow hotel.

She jokes her onscreen character has varied inspirations from Farrah Fawcett in Charlie's Angels to Daphne in Scooby Doo, and this week's shows promise to be some of the biggest in her life.

Hayter also feels AEW itself could feature more women's wrestling - the promotion has yet to headline a major supercard with a women's match in its existence.

"Women in wrestling have proven themselves - we can do great matches, good promos and make you want to see a match.

"There's some inherent misogyny in wrestling as a whole, and women wrestlers for years would always get common tropes.

"But there are lots of different flavours of women's wrestling, and we can tap into that more."

Hayter herself says she's ready for any of those flavours, whatever comes next.

"I think I'm someone that just rolls with the punches. Whatever comes next I'll go full force with it."

Yamaha Outdoor Access Initiative Awards Over $225,000 in Q2 2026 Grants

Funding Supports Youth Outdoor Education, Trail Stewardship, and Responsible Motorized Recreation

MARIETTA, Ga. – August 25, 2026 – Yamaha Motor Corp., USA, awarded more than $225,000 in second-quarter funding through the Yamaha Outdoor Access Initiative (Yamaha OAI), supporting seven organizations working to expand responsible access to outdoor and motorized recreation through youth education, trail stewardship, ride area safety improvements, and enhanced access opportunities.

The latest grants fund projects ranging from youth boating, fishing, and bicycling education to trail rehabilitation, new trail development, improved wayfinding, and track and riding-area safety. The quarter also brings together Yamaha OAI and Yamaha Rightwaters to help expand outdoor recreation opportunities for young people through boating and fishing programs on California's Catalina Island.

"This quarter's recipients demonstrate the many ways responsible recreation and long-term outdoor access go hand-in-hand, from introducing young people to lifelong outdoor activities to maintaining the trails and riding areas enthusiasts depend on," said Steve Nessl, Yamaha Motorsports marketing director. "We're also proud to continue our support of All Kids Bike for a fifth year, helping give kindergarteners at more than 50 elementary schools nationwide the opportunity to learn how to ride a bike through their physical education programs."

Q2 2026 Yamaha Outdoor Access Initiative Grant Recipients

Yamaha OAI awarded grants to the following organizations during the second-quarter funding cycle:

Catalina Outdoor Adventure Club (RJ Nautical, Avalon, Calif.) received funding, along with a 40-horsepower outboard motor contributed by Yamaha Rightwaters, to expand youth boating and fishing programs on Catalina Island.

GARTRA – Georgia Recreational Trail Riders Association (Nelson Powersports, Blue Ridge, Ga.) received funding to support trail maintenance at seven OHV areas throughout Georgia.

Quad Cities ATV Club (Five Seasons Sports, Eveleth, Minn.) will rehabilitate two heavily used trails that connect riders to a regional trail system in northern Minnesota.

San Luis Valley Great Outdoors (Peak Motor Sports, Alamosa, Colo.) will develop a new connector trail and improve wayfinding signage in Colorado's San Luis Valley.

Strider Education Foundation / All Kids Bike will expand its Kindergarten PE Learn-to-Ride Program to 12 additional schools nationwide, continuing a partnership with Yamaha OAI that began in 2021.

Summit County Off-Road Riders (SCORR) (Silverthorne Powersports, Silverthorne, Colo.) will make track maintenance and safety improvements at its motocross facility in Dillon, Colorado.

West Central Montana Avalanche Foundation (Five Valley Honda Yamaha, Missoula, Mont.) will support backcountry trail maintenance and safety education for motorized recreation in the Seeley Lake region.

Yamaha OAI accepts applications year-round and awards grants quarterly to eligible organizations working to improve access to outdoor recreation. The program prioritizes projects that promote safe and responsible motorized recreation, maintain and improve trails and riding areas, and help protect sustainable access to public lands.

The application deadline for Q3 2026 grants is September 30, 2026. Public land managers, riding clubs, land stewardship organizations, and outdoor recreation groups are encouraged to learn more and apply at YamahaOAI.com.

Follow Yamaha Outdoors on social media at @YamahaOutdoors and share your adventures using #Yamaha, #YamahaOAI, #REALizeYourAdventure, and #ProvenOffRoad.

About the Yamaha Outdoor Access Initiative

Since 2008, the Yamaha Outdoor Access Initiative has led the powersports industry in supporting responsible access to our nation's public lands for outdoor enthusiasts. With more than $8 million contributed to over 575 projects across the country, Yamaha has directly and indirectly supported thousands of miles of motorized recreation trails, maintained and rehabilitated riding and hunting areas, improved staging areas, supplied organizations with essential OHV safety education, built bridges over fish-bearing streams, helped children learn to ride bicycles, and partnered with local outdoor enthusiast communities to improve access to public lands. Each quarter, Yamaha accepts applications from nonprofit or tax-exempt organizations, including OHV riding and cycling clubs and associations, national, state, and local public land-use agencies, outdoor enthusiast associations, and land conservation groups with an interest in protecting, improving, expanding, and/or maintaining access for safe, responsible, and sustainable public use.

For updated guidelines, the application form, and the latest Outdoor Access Initiative news, please visit YamahaOAI.com. If you have specific inquiries about the Yamaha Outdoor Access Initiative, you can reach the dedicated hotline at 1-877-OHV-TRAIL (877-648-8724), email OHVAccess@Yamaha-Motor.com, or send correspondence to:

Yamaha Outdoor Access Initiative 3065 Chastain Meadows Parkway, Bldg. 100 Marietta, GA 30066

articles.body:
Angel Reese and the Atlanta Dream are in the midst of a four-game winning streak, and on Monday night, in a win over the Los Angeles Sparks , Reese etched her name in the history books. Reese snagged a record-breaking 26 rebounds in the game, the most dominant performance on the glass in the WNBA's 30-year history.

Reese also recorded yet another double-double, scoring 11 points in the contest. However, the manner in which she scored her final bucket has been deemed "unethical" by some fans.

With the outcome already decided and less than 20 seconds remaining in regulation, Reese was camped out back at the Dream's basket rather than running back to defend with her teammates, which left her wide open to collect an outlet pass and reach double-digit scoring.

"We all know Angel Reese just wants her double double and look how she gets it. Cherry picking per usual. If she doesn't get to the free throw line or cherry pick, she can't score. It's all about her and only her," posted one person on X who wan't a fan of her tactics.

We all know Angel Reese just wants her double double and look how she gets it. Cherry picking per usual. If she doesn’t get to the free throw line or cherry pick, she can’t score. It’s all about her and only her. pic.twitter.com/DS0WlKPD8u — HeHateMe (@_HeHateMee_) August 25, 2026

— HeHateMe (@_HeHateMee_) August 25, 2026

The original poster wasn't alone in his criticisms of Reese.

"Even half the time she does this she blows the layup and can't score. Shoots under 50% from within a couple ft of the basket. How's that even possible? Great rebounder but she's absolutely unskilled," one fan posted on X.

"What a low IQ and selfish play. Up 7 with 15 seconds left and she doesn't run the clock out?" someone else posted.

There's no denying that Reese's offensive game needs some polishing, but even so, her impact is undeniable. Reese is on a surefire path to ending up in the Hall of Fame, and with the Dream peaking right before the playoffs, she might even beat her rival Caitlin Clark to a WNBA championship.

articles.body: NEW DELHI: New York City mayor Zohran Mamdani has said he does not support a planned event featuring RSS chief Mohan Bhagwat at Madison Square Garden, while noting that the city may not have the legal authority to stop the private gathering.Bhagwat is scheduled to address around 5,000 members of the Indian diaspora at the iconic New York venue on August 29. His visit to the United States is part of the Rashtriya Swayamsevak Sangh's centenary-year global outreach programme."I don't support the rally, but I don't know if the city has any jurisdiction on cancelling a private event,â Mamdani said at a news conference on Tuesday.Mamdani was responding to questions about the RSS, the proposed event and protests against Bhagwat's appearance. He was also asked whether the gathering should be cancelled.The mayor, who is the first Indian-American to hold the post in New York City, said his views were influenced partly by his family background.âI also stand here as the first Indian-American Mayor in our city's history, and my mother's family is all still in India," Mamdani said.He said his understanding of India was based on the idea of a society where people of different backgrounds could belong equally.He said the vision of India that he was taught by his family and the one that he grew up being very familiar with was that of "a pluralistic society, of a secular republic that believed in the belonging of each and every person who was from India".Mamdani said he was opposed to what he described as an increasingly exclusionary political movement.âAnd it has been incredibly troubling to see the rise of a movement that is predicated on an exclusionary vision of any country, frankly, and so it is one that I find myself in deep opposition to, not only as an Indian-American but also as the Mayor of a city that believes deeply in the belonging of each and every person, no matter their colour, their creed, their religion, their faith, wherever they're from,â Mamdani said.Protests planned over Bhagwat eventThe planned appearance has faced opposition from several interfaith and civil rights organisations. Groups including Hindus for Human Rights, the Indian American Muslim Council and the Interfaith Centre of New York held a press conference outside New York City Hall and called for the event to be cancelled.Bhagwat arrived in the US on Tuesday as part of the RSS's centenary-year outreach. articles.title: The Voice Lindsay Clancy Says Told Her to Kill Lasted Just 18 Minutes. A Psychologist Says That’s ‘Very, Very Unusual’
articles.summary: Clancy is charged with the murders of her three children — Cora, 5, Dawson, 3, and 8-month-old Callan
articles.body:
Lindsay Clancy is accused of intentionally killing her three young children

Her defense attorney has argued that she was not criminally responsible because she was suffering from postpartum psychosis

A forensic psychologist testified that Clancy said a male voice told her, "This is your last chance. You have to kill the kids so you can kill yourself"

A psychologist testified that Lindsay Clancy reported hearing a male voice for the first and only time during the roughly 18 minutes the killings of her three children occurred.

"She only experienced it for the 18 minutes or so that it took to kill the children," Kirk Heilbrun, who evaluated the mother of three, testified on Monday, August 24, the Boston Globe reported. "And to put it mildly, that would be a very, very unusual pattern or manifestation of how this kind of thing comes about."

Heilbrun told the court that Clancy said the male voice told her, "This is your last chance. You have to kill the kids so you can kill yourself."

Heilbrun said the timing was unusual and said it could be a way to lessen her culpability.

Prosecutors allege Clancy deliberately strangled her three children — Cora, 5, Dawson, 3, and 8-month-old Callan — with exercise bands at their Duxbury, Mass., home in January 2023.

After killing the children, she jumped out of a second-story window in an apparent suicide attempt, leaving her paralyzed.

Clancy, 36, does not deny she killed her children.

Her defense attorney has argued that she was not criminally responsible because she was suffering from postpartum psychosis at the time of the murders.

Want to keep up with the latest crime coverage? Sign up for PEOPLE's free True Crime newsletter for breaking crime news, ongoing trial coverage and details of intriguing unsolved cases.

Heilbrun also testified that Clancy killed her children because she thought the children would suffer without her and that killing them would allow them to be "together in heaven."

During testimony on Tuesday, August 25, forensic psychiatrist Gregory Saathoff, testified that Clancy, who he interviewed twice in 2026, told him she first killed her son Dawson, then Cora and then her youngest child.

"All during this time where this voice is over and over, over again saying, "This is your last chance. You have to kill the children before you kill yourself," he testified.

Asked by a prosecutor if there was significance to the fact that the voice told her to kill the children, but did not tell her how to kill them, he responded, "Yes."

"You know, just like adults, children have a will to survive — a strong, strong will to survive. I think it's just part of being human," Saathoff said. "I mean, they are active. They can walk. They can run."

The closely watched four-week trial held in Plymouth County Superior Court has drawn national attention and sparked debate about postpartum mental health and the treatment of women experiencing psychiatric crises.

More than 70 witnesses have testified during the proceedings including medical experts, friends, law enforcement and Clancy's ex-husband Patrick.

articles.title: As Clancy trial unfolds, AHN program offers hope for mothers in crisis
articles.summary: As the Lindsay Clancy trial unfolds, Pittsburgh experts and advocates say early intervention and specialized care can save families.
articles.body:
As the Lindsay Clancy trial brings national attention to postpartum psychosis, Allegheny Health Network is highlighting its efforts to support mothers experiencing perinatal mood disorders.

The Alexis Joy D'Achille Center for Perinatal Mental Health , established in 2018, offers integrated care for women experiencing postpartum depression and anxiety. The center was named after Alexis Joy D'Achille, who died in 2013 after struggling with postpartum depression.

Her husband, Steven D'Achille, founded the Alexis Joy D'Achille Foundation to raise awareness and support for maternal mental health and postpartum care.

The center's treatment model includes intensive outpatient therapy that allows mothers and babies to stay together during care. It also offers support for partners and families.

"Women need support from their family and women need to stay together with their children," D'Achille said. "The quicker they get that help and the less scary it is and the more support they have, the quicker they recover and get their life back."

Dr. Ewurama Sackey, medical director of Women's Behavioral Health at AHN, said postpartum psychosis is a medical emergency that requires immediate attention.

"That's why sometimes it's really hard to detect because someone can seem like themselves one minute and then the next minute not," Sackey said. "From what we know, we know it's an emergency. We know it needs to be dealt with right away, and we know that it's treatable."

The center has served more than 18,000 patients and handled more than 24,000 referrals since opening. The program is one of a few in the country that offers intensive mother-baby outpatient care.

D'Achille said he hopes the program can serve as a model for other health systems.

"This is a story that happens every day in every city in America," he said. "Women deserve more. We as a country can do more and we should do more."

articles.title: Trump administration plans mass visa revocations for people seeking asylum
articles.summary: A sweeping new effort would affect people who entered the U.S. as temporary visitors before seeking asylum, further narrowing access to protection.
articles.body:
The Trump administration plans to revoke visas from people who entered the United States legally as tourists or business travelers and later applied for asylum – opening a new front in its campaign to restrict access to humanitarian protection.

The Department of State is coordinating with the Department of Homeland Security to identify people who arrived on B-1 or B-2 visas and subsequently sought asylum in a move aimed at "making clear that a visa is a privilege – not a right," State Department spokesperson Tommy Pigott said in a statement to USA TODAY.

"These types of visas are issued with the clear understanding that they are for those who intend to return home," Pigott added. "Obtaining a visa in order to seek asylum is fraud – which is grounds for visa revocation. This is an ongoing process as we uphold the integrity of our visa and asylum laws."

The State Department has not explained how it will determine whether people obtained a visa intending to apply for asylum. It also hasn't detailed how it will figure out whether visa-holders decided to seek protection later because conditions in their home countries or their personal circumstances changed. Pigott also did not specify how many people would be affected, saying the number of revocations "remains dynamic" and that they would occur on a rolling basis.

The Associated Press, which first reported the administration's plans, said as many as 200,000 visas issued between 2016 and 2026 could be revoked, citing State Department documents and two U.S. officials. If carried out on that scale, according to the AP, it would be the largest single mass visa revocation in U.S. history.

When Luis and his mother fled Venezuela in 2017, they boarded a flight to Florida with visitor visas in hand. Luis, whom USA TODAY is identifying only by his first name because he fears that speaking publicly could jeopardize his asylum case, said they were determined to follow the law even as they sought safety.

Luis, 26, said he had been wounded and threatened by security officials amid the Venezuelan government's violent crackdown on protests, in which scores of people were killed. Soon after arriving, Luis and his mother applied for asylum, believing they had done "everything by the book," he said. Then they waited. Nearly nine years later, his case remains unresolved.

"And there's nothing I can do until USCIS moves my case," he said. "This is out of my hands, and, trust me, if I could, I would choose anything over this anxiety-inducing waiting game. But going home is simply not an option."

Now, Luis fears the path he chose because he believed it was legal could be used as evidence that he broke the law – and that his request for protection could make him a target.

It remains unclear what the revocation plans would mean for Luis or others with pending asylum claims. However, experts said revoking a visa alone may have little impact on someone already in the country. A visa allows a foreign national to travel to a U.S. port of entry and request admission; revoking it would generally prevent the person from using it to return to the U.S., but would not, on its own, cancel a pending asylum application.

"The action has very little effect," said David Bier, director of immigration studies at the Cato Institute, a libertarian think tank.

The move could carry greater consequences, if DHS separately cancels any immigration status the person holds, he said, potentially exposing some applicants to arrest by Immigration and Customs Enforcement.

Neither agency has said whether the revocations will be accompanied by changes to applicants' immigration status, formal fraud findings, removal proceedings or other enforcement actions. When reached for comment, DHS referred USA TODAY to the State Department.

Dara Lind, a senior fellow at the American Immigration Council – an immigrant rights groups – said the practical reach may be smaller than the figure reported by the AP suggests. Some visas issued as far back as 2016 may have expired, she said, and it is unclear how many people would lose an immigration status on which they still rely. The announcement, she said, may function partly as a "scare tactic," sowing fear among asylum seekers, even if its immediate legal consequences remain limited.

"It's not super clear where on the scale of saber-rattling – just declaring that they don't like things – versus actually materially changing a lot of people's circumstances this particular thing is," she said.

But Lind said the initiative sends a broader message about the administration's efforts to make seeking asylum increasingly untenable.

"What is the right way to apply for asylum in the U.S. right now, according to the Trump administration?" Lind said.

Applying affirmatively through USCIS has traditionally been regarded as a lawful way to seek protection, she said, yet the administration is now seeking to penalize some immigrants for doing precisely that.

"It's another kind of demonstration that they are doing everything they can to keep applying for asylum from being something that allows you to stay in the United States," Lind said.

Rooted in international protections developed after World War II, the modern U.S. asylum system was established through the Refugee Act of 1980. It allows people facing persecution because of their race, religion, nationality, political opinion or membership in a particular social group to seek protection. Under federal law, a person must be physically present in the United States or arriving at its border to apply for asylum. The law allows people to seek that protection regardless of their immigration status.

But the visa initiative follows years of mounting political tension over asylum, particularly after the U.S. experienced historically high levels of migration at the southern border during the Biden administration. Many of those arriving sought asylum, putting pressure on a system that has been backlogged for a decade and fueling criticism that applicants could remain in the country for years while their cases were decided.

Administration officials have pointed to those concerns to justify the new visa crackdown.

"People in the US and all over the world are fed up with bogus asylum claims," Deputy Secretary of State Christopher Landau wrote Monday on X. "Asylum isn't supposed to be a loophole to circumvent immigration law."

President Joe Biden imposed his own restrictions on asylum access in 2024 as border crossings became a defining political vulnerability. Donald Trump campaigned on going much further, promising to halt illegal immigration and carry out mass deportations.

Since last year, Trump has pursued a series of actions intended to restrict access to asylum and accelerate removals. On his first day back in office, he issued a proclamation declaring crossings at the southern border an "invasion" and sought to prevent many immigrants arriving there from applying for asylum.

In April, a federal appeals court ruled that the administration could not categorically bar people already in the country from applying for asylum or circumvent the removal procedures established by Congress. Federal law, the court wrote , gives people physically present in the United States a right to apply, regardless of their status or whether they arrived at an official port of entry.

By the end of fiscal 2025, more than 1.4 million affirmative asylum applications were pending before U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services, according to DHS . Separately, about 2.3 million people with formal asylum applications were awaiting hearings or decisions in immigration court as of June, according to data from the Transactional Records Access Clearinghouse , a nonprofit data gathering organization at Syracuse University.

A pending asylum application does not itself confer lawful immigration status or prevent someone from being placed in removal proceedings. Still, asylum seekers were generally allowed to remain in the country while their claims were adjudicated and, after meeting eligibility requirements, could obtain authorization to work. Under previous administrations, applicants without criminal records were typically not prioritized for arrest or detention.

That has changed under Trump. Federal immigration agents have detained people with pending claims at immigration courthouses and during routine ICE check-ins – appointments they were required to attend as part of their cases.

The administration has also reshaped the courts deciding many asylum cases. The Justice Department has fired immigration judges , appointed some military lawyers to serve as temporary immigration judges and increasingly turned to mass hearings as it seeks to push cases through more quickly.

Though asylum denial rates had been slowly rising since late 2023, they have surged under Trump, TRAC data shows . In September 2023, fewer than half of applicants were denied. By June 2026, the latest month available, the denial rate had reached 94.1 percent.

Lind said the government is increasingly targeting immigrants who have spent years complying with its requirements – filing applications, renewing work permits, paying fees and reporting changes of address – only to remain trapped in a backlog they cannot control.

"You don't need to know the ins and outs of immigration law to know that so many of the people who have been most harmed by this administration are people who have spent years of their lives making sure that they check all the boxes, dot all the i's and cross all the t's," she said.

"None of these people would have pending applications if USCIS were processing applications in a timely fashion," Lind added. "Instead of actually putting any effort toward adjudicating those cases, they're doing all of these things that are punishing the people who have been waiting in line."

The crackdown on asylum seekers comes as the U.S. government has also made it more difficult and expensive to enter or remain in the country through legal channels.

The State Department said this month that it had revoked more than 175,000 visas since Trump returned to office, mostly following law enforcement encounters. Other revocations involved alleged visa violations, fraud, calls for violence or national security threats. The administration has expanded social media screening, targeted foreign students accused of antisemitic activity and revoked more than 600 visas through a task force focused on alleged "birth tourism."

It has also required a $100,000 payment for certain new work visa petitions and moved to limit how long foreign students, exchange visitors and journalists may remain in the country.

For nearly nine years, Luis said, he has renewed his work permit, complied with the government's requirements and waited for it to decide whether he can remain in the country where he sought refuge.

He thought entering with a visa and applying through the asylum system meant he was following the rules. Now, he said, doing everything the government asked of him has not made him feel safe.

"It feels like you're being hunted," Luis said. "And my only 'crime' is seeking the American dream."

articles.title: Teen Claims She Had a ‘Bad Day’ Before Fatally Shooting Milwaukee Mother in Road Rage Incident: DA
articles.summary: Mariah Ruiz, 18, has been charged in connection with the killing of Minerva Hernandez-Lopez, 44, after a verbal altercation escalated on Aug. 17
articles.body:
Mariah Ruiz, 18, is accused of shooting her 44-year-old mother, Minerva Hernandez-Lopez, after a road rage argument in Milwaukee, according to a criminal complaint obtained by PEOPLE

Ruiz admitted to the shooting, police say, claiming she had a "bad day" and later wrote an apology to the victim's family

If convicted, Ruiz could face up to 65 years in prison

A Milwaukee teen has been accused of killing a 44-year-old mother in a road rage incident after having a bad day.

Mariah Ruiz, 18, has been charged with first-degree reckless homicide by use of a dangerous weapon, according to online records viewed by PEOPLE on Monday, Aug. 24.

The incident occurred on the afternoon of Aug. 17, when Ruiz is accused of engaging in a verbal altercation with Minerva Hernandez-Lopez that later turned deadly, according to a criminal complaint filed in Milwaukee County Circuit Court and obtained by PEOPLE.

PEOPLE has reached out to an attorney for Ruiz, but did not immediately receive a response.

Ruiz allegedly cut Hernandez-Lopez off while she and a 16-year-old friend were on their way to a grocery store, before the verbal altercation ensued. At some point, Hernandez-Lopez allegedly "flicked [Ruiz] off," Ruiz told investigators, according to the criminal complaint.

Hernandez-Lopez allegedly told Ruiz, "Little girl, you need to drive," the 16-year-old told investigators, according to the complaint.

The witness said Ruiz allegedly replied by threatening to call U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) on Hernandez-Lopez after the victim yelled at her in Spanish, before the situation intensified, per the complaint. Ruiz also told investigators she "threatened to call ICE on the victim," the complaint reads.

Ruiz is then accused of pulling out a gun and following Hernandez-Lopez after their argument.

Hernandez-Lopez's tan GMC was reportedly seen on video backing into Ruiz's front bumper of her Nissan before Ruiz allegedly opened fire, according to the criminal complaint. Five bullet casings were recovered from the scene, where Hernandez-Lopez was pronounced dead.

"We tried everything we could do to help her," Jesus Ferreira, a witness, told WISN in an on-camera interview. "It's something traumatic [that] I've never seen."

The Milwaukee Medical Examiner's Office completed an autopsy, and said Hernandez-Lopez's cause of death was listed as a gunshot wound to the neck and the manner of death was homicide, according to the complaint.

The teen told authorities that she was having a "bad day" after fighting with her mother, the complaint alleges.

Want to keep up with the latest crime coverage? Sign up for PEOPLE's free True Crime newsletter for breaking crime news, ongoing trial coverage and details of intriguing unsolved cases.

Police say Ruiz admitted to shooting and killing Hernandez-Lopez and wrote a letter of apology to the victim's family.

Ruiz, who turned herself in, "stated that she did not mean to hurt the victim and she is not sure why she did it," according to the complaint. She also told investigators that her 16-year-old friend told her not to shoot at the time of the alleged attack.

If convicted, Ruiz could face 65 years in prison.

A cash bond of $100,000 was set for Ruiz. She is scheduled for a preliminary hearing on Friday, Aug. 28.

articles.title: Woman, 51, Dies After an 8-Hour Plastic Surgery Procedure
articles.summary: A 51-year-old woman has died after undergoing extensive plastic surgery for her face and neck. Andreia Vieira Gaspar had saved up for years for her “dream” m...
articles.body:
A 51-year-old woman has died after undergoing extensive plastic surgery for her face and neck.

Andreia Vieira Gaspar had saved up for years for her "dream" mix of six plastic surgery procedures, The U.S. Sun reported on Monday. The combination of procedures cost around £17,000, or $23,000.

Gaspar died only hours after undergoing the eight-hour procedure on Aug. 12.

Gaspar, a businesswoman from Brazil, had lived in Spain for five years but flew to her home country to undergo plastic surgery at Hospital Ankar in Goiânia.

Her operation included a deep-plane facelift and a blepharoplasty, also known as an eyelid lift, during which surgeons remove fat and excess skin from the eyelids.

She also underwent a forehead lift, also known as a brow lift, neck liposuction, and bony genioplasty : a surgery to reshape the chin.

Gaspar's plastic surgery also included nanofat injections. This usually involves the surgeon harvesting the patient's fat, purifying it, and injecting it back into her face to improve skin texture and diminish the appearance of fine lines.

According to her family, Gaspar's health deteriorated quickly after she left the hospital, and she experienced extreme pain.

Her sister, Djiane Vieira, told Brazilian TV station TV Anhanguera that Gaspar's tongue swelled so much she was unable to close her mouth, and she struggled to breathe, according to The Daily Mail .

Vieira claimed to have texted her sister's medical team telling them her sister was "dying." The family also claimed that the hospital did not have an intensive care unit or ambulance available.

When the medics arrived, they were unable to save Gaspar.

According to her family, a medical report listed Gaspar's cause of death as acute thrombosis and pulmonary infarction. Acute thrombosis refers to a blood clot that blocks blood flow, and pulmonary infarction refers to the death of lung tissue when its blood supply is cut off.

The Goiás Public Prosecutor's Office has asked for a police investigation to be opened into possible involuntary manslaughter, according to The U.S. Sun.

According to the outlet, the doctor who performed Gaspar's plastic surgeries, Dr. Lessandro Martins, said he "sympathizes with the pain of her family," but is confident "the investigation will demonstrate that the care provided was appropriate".

Hospital Ankar's lawyer, Cristiene Pereira Couto, told the outlet: "The patient received immediate emergency treatment, with medical and nursing staff providing care and taking the necessary measures in response to her condition."

The attorney also said that once the emergency happened, the patient was attended to immediately. "She was promptly attended to by the staff present, who used the necessary hospital facilities and carried out the appropriate emergency measures."

The hospital also said Gaspar's pre-surgery evaluation was performed externally.

articles.title: Woman and Husband Accused of Murdering Her Lover, a Beloved Teacher — Leaving 2 Kids Stranded in Mexico
articles.summary: Geoffrey Bernardi’s mother says Misty Gomez, who is now charged in connection with his death, wept at his hospital bedside and said, “We have to find who did...
articles.body:
Geoffrey Bernardi was found severely beaten near a California canal and died less than two days later

U.S. Marshals arrested Misty Gomez and Antonio Garcia in Mexico following an eight-month investigation

The suspects are married, police say, but Gomez was also Bernardi's girlfriend

A married couple accused of killing the wife's boyfriend were arrested in Mexico following an eight-month investigation into the California teacher's fatal beating.

Antonio Garcia, 40, and his wife, Misty Gomez, 32, were taken into custody on Aug. 19 and extradited to California in connection with the December 2025 death of 37-year-old Geoffrey Bernardi, the Clovis Police Department announced .

Police said Gomez was dating Bernardi while married to Garcia. Investigators identified the couple as suspects after uncovering evidence and communications between them, according to the department.

Bernardi was found apparently severely beaten and alone near a canal shortly before 1 a.m. on Dec. 18, 2025, police said in an earlier release. He was transported to a hospital, where he died less than two days later.

Want to keep up with the latest crime coverage? Sign up for PEOPLE's free True Crime newsletter for breaking crime news, ongoing trial coverage and details of intriguing unsolved cases.

Bernardi's mother, Erin Adams, told ABC30 that her son had been dating Gomez for only a few months and did not know she was married.

"The first time he went out with her, he told me, 'I met the woman I'm going to marry,'" Adams recalled. "We didn't know she was already married."

Adams alleged that Gomez called her on the night of the attack to say Bernardi had been severely beaten, then joined the family at his hospital bedside the following day.

"She lay on his bed and wept and said, 'We have to find who did this to him,'" Adams told the outlet. "And, you know, she was playing a game. She was watching our grief."

Adams said her son had been beaten "beyond recognition" and died just weeks before his 38th birthday. She also claimed the family suspected Gomez was involved within two days of the attack.

By January, police had determined that the assault was not random and identified a person of interest, ABC30 reported. Authorities ultimately used unspecified technology to track Gomez and Garcia to Mexico, where police said they had been hiding for months.

Gomez fled the country with her two daughters from previous relationships, who had been reported missing from Dinuba in April, police said. The girls' families told ABC30 that the children, ages 9 and 12, remain in the custody of Mexico's National System for Integral Family Development in Michoacán as their relatives work to bring them home.

Garcia and Gomez were initially booked into the Santa Rita Jail in Alameda County before being transferred Monday to the Fresno County Jail, according to ABC30. A criminal complaint obtained by the outlet accuses both defendants of murdering Bernardi "with malice aforethought."

Bernardi worked in career technical education for the Clovis Unified School District. According to his obituary, he was an experienced stagehand and sound technician who loved theater, music and the arts. In recent years, he worked as an AV design technician, helping run the theater for Clovis Unified productions.

"He was growing in a job he loved, working with people he loved," the obituary said. "He was happy and thriving."

Both defendants' bail was initially set at $1 million, ABC30 reported.

articles.title: A Virginia university fought against its first gay student group — and lost. Now it’s honoring them
articles.summary: Virginia Commonwealth University will unveil a historical marker honoring the students whose landmark court victory expanded constitutional protections for L...
articles.body:
Virginia Commonwealth University leaders tried more than 50 years ago to prevent the formation of their school's first gay student group. Now, the organization's history will be honored with a historical marker.

VCU will unveil the commemorative marker on campus in October, according to Richmond ABC affiliate WRIC . It will recount the history of VCU's Gay Alliance of Students, which was founded in 1974. The university initially rejected the organization's application for official recognition, leading to a two-year court battle that ended with a federal appeals court ruling that the school had violated the students' constitutional rights.

The landmark Gay Alliance of Students v. Matthews decision opened the door for similar student organizations at colleges and universities throughout the federal judicial circuit that includes Virginia, Maryland , North Carolina , South Carolina and West Virginia . The organization has celebrated the 50th anniversary of its court victory throughout the last year.

Related : Emails reveal Virginia school officials approved an LGBTQ+ club — until conservative backlash hit

The commemoration will culminate with a gala and an October 16 unveiling of the historical marker, whose text has been approved by the Virginia Department of Historic Resources:

"A group of students at Virginia Commonwealth University (VCU) in Richmond established in September 1974 the Gay Alliance of Students, the university's first openly LGBTQ+ student organization. A legal battle that attracted local and national support for the Alliance ensued after VCU rejected its application for official recognition. The U.S. Court of Appeals for the Fourth Circuit ruled in Gay Alliance of Students v. Matthews in October 1976 that VCU's refusal to recognize the organization violated the First and Fourteenth Amendments of the U.S. Constitution. The court's decision set a legal precedent. It extended protections to similar student groups in Virginia, Maryland, North Carolina, South Carolina, and West Virginia."

Related : A rural Virginia school board changed its rules to block an LGBTQ+ club. Students are suing in federal court

The half-century-old fight echoes today in another federal courtroom in Richmond. Two students and their families sued the King George County School Board this month after officials blocked a proposed Gay-Straight Alliance at King George Middle School while continuing to allow other noncurricular groups.

The lawsuit alleges that officials repeatedly changed the rules in response to opposition to the GSA, violating the students' First Amendment rights and the federal Equal Access Act. The families are asking a judge to order the district to allow the organization to operate on the same terms as other student groups.

Related : A Virginia school board bent over backward to block an LGBTQ+ club. One mom explains why she's suing

University officials hope the marker will signal that VCU welcomes everyone — decades after its leaders tried to deny LGBTQ+ students official representation.

"I hope that when students and alumni see this marker, they understand that VCU is for everyone, and that students' voices and alumni voices matter," said Josh Leidy, director of affinity programs in VCU's Office of Development and Alumni Relations, in a statement released by VCU . "The Gay Alliance of Students case only came about because students had the courage to stand up and advocate for what needed to happen for the community."

articles.title: A couple built a four-bedroom home in Wiltshire for their disabled daughter in 2022, now face council demolition order after planning row over basement and Green Belt rules
articles.summary: UK News: A Wiltshire couple have been ordered to demolish the four-bedroom home they have lived in with their disabled daughter for more than four years after .
articles.body: A Wiltshire couple have been ordered to demolish the four-bedroom home they have lived in with their disabled daughter for more than four years after a planning dispute over the property's basement and decking.According to a report published by The Wiltshire Gazette and Herald, Pim and Sheree de Witte built the hillside property at Little Orchard in Kingdown, between Corsham and Bath. The house, which replaced an earlier dwelling on the site, was completed and occupied in 2022.The couple are now appealing to the Planning Inspectorate after Wiltshire Council refused retrospective planning permission for the house as built. The appeal has put the enforcement notice requiring demolition on hold.Couple say basement was needed for disabled daughterThe de Wittes were originally granted planning permission in 2019 for a replacement dwelling with ground and first-floor levels. However, the completed property included an additional basement level and a decking area.The couple say the basement was constructed as part of the foundations for engineering reasons and was not an arbitrary addition. They subsequently converted the space into residential accommodation for their disabled daughter.They argue that the property remains a replacement dwelling rather than a new-build home and maintain that the original planning permission was lawfully implemented.The couple have also argued that the need to provide suitable accommodation for their disabled daughter should be considered a "material consideration" in the planning decision.Council says house breaches Green Belt policyThe property is located within the Green Belt, and Wiltshire Council has argued that the house as built is materially larger than the dwelling it replaced.A planning application submitted in 2024 seeking to regularise the changes was refused.The couple returned to the council in 2025 with another proposal. Under the revised plans, part of the basement floor area would have been sealed off and concealed by depositing soil around it. The size of the decking would also have been reduced.However, the council rejected the proposal, saying the dwelling remained materially larger than the one it replaced and conflicted with Green Belt policy.The council also said the application failed to demonstrate material considerations or special circumstances that could outweigh the harm identified.Couple call council's approach "harsh and punitive"The de Wittes have criticised the council's decision, describing its response as "unnecessarily harsh and punitive given the individual circumstances and merits of this case."They have now taken their case to the Planning Inspectorate, which will consider whether the property can remain.The couple have also proposed alternative solutions if their appeal is dismissed, including reinstating the house to its previously approved form.Demolition order put on holdIn February this year, the couple were ordered to demolish the property by the end of August. articles.title: Some allowed to return after Hawk Fire destroys homes in Reno area
articles.summary: The blaze has destroyed 47 homes, and containment was at 27% Tuesday, officials said. There have been no deaths, which the fire chief called “incredible” for how fast it moved.
articles.body: Around 9,000 people have been cleared to return to their Reno, Nevada, area homes Tuesday as firefighters made more progress containing a major, human-caused wildfire that destroyed more than 40 homes, officials said. Around 5,000 people were still evacuated because of the Hawk Fire, which began Saturday and grew quickly, Washoe County Sheriff Darin Balaam said at a news conference. But by 2 p.m., residents in the areas east of State Route 395 were allowed to return, Balaam said. The west side of the highway was the hardest hit, he said. The fire has burned 15,067 acres, and it was 27% contained Tuesday afternoon, officials said at a news conference. No deaths have been reported in the fire, which Richard Edwards, fire chief of the Truckee Meadows Fire Protection District, said was remarkable. “I think it’s incredible that we’ve not had a fatality in this fire, given how fast it’s moved,” he said. The fire moved six miles within 24 hours of its start Saturday, Edwards said. The cause of the fire, which is believed to have been human-caused, remains under investigation, said Balaam, the sheriff. It was not known Tuesday whether it was intentional or accidental, he said. “We can say that because of where it occurred,” Balaam said. “It was in the middle of nowhere. There was no lightning strikes. There was nothing else that could have caused this fire.” While firefighters have made progress, critical fire weather conditions were forecast to begin Wednesday and last through the weekend, Edwards said. “Please be careful,” he said. “All of these fires, these large fires that we’ve incurred over the last 2½ weeks, which — human-caused — that means they’re preventable.”

articles.title: He Offered to Help an 89-Year-Old With His Phone, Then Prosecutors Say $100,000 Moved Into His Crypto Accounts
articles.summary: An 89-year-old California man thought a new friend was helping him with his phone and other technology. Prosecutors say that relationship instead gave the yo...
articles.body:
An 89-year-old California man thought a new friend was helping him with his phone and other technology. Prosecutors say that relationship instead gave the younger man access to financial accounts that were eventually drained of nearly $100,000.

William Bao Khoa Ly, 26, of Simi Valley, met the Thousand Oaks resident in June 2024 and offered to help him with electronic devices, according to the Ventura County District Attorney's Office .

Ly began visiting the man two or three times a week. Prosecutors say he eventually obtained the victim's cellphone PIN and used that access to reach both his bank and cryptocurrency accounts.

Over the following 14 months, authorities allege 91 transactions moved nearly $100,000 from the man's bank account into cryptocurrency accounts owned or controlled by Ly. The victim's bank later recovered more than $50,000.

The Friendship Gave Him Access to the Victim's Phone

The District Attorney's Office says Ly presented himself as someone who was proficient with technology and could help the older man with his devices.

As the relationship developed, he became a frequent visitor to the victim's home. Prosecutors allege those visits eventually gave Ly access to the PIN used to unlock the man's cellphone.

Earlier reporting from the Ventura County Sheriff's Office said Ly also helped reset the password to the man's Coinbase cryptocurrency account, which was linked directly to his bank account, according to KTLA .

Prosecutors Counted 91 Transactions Over 14 Months

From June 2024 through August 2025, prosecutors allege Ly conducted 91 separate transfers involving the victim's money. The funds moved from the bank account into cryptocurrency accounts that authorities say Ly owned or controlled.

An earlier Sheriff's Office investigation described more than $97,000 moving through more than 80 transactions. The newer charging announcement provides the updated count of 91 transactions and describes the total as nearly $100,000.

The Bank Recovered More Than Half of the Money

The Ventura County Sheriff's Office began investigating after the suspected theft was reported in November 2025. Financial crimes detectives worked with the FBI and the Ventura County Fraud Working Group to obtain records tracing the transfers into accounts and cryptocurrency wallets investigators associated with Ly. Prosecutors say the victim's bank ultimately recovered more than $50,000.

Ly Pleaded Not Guilty to Three Felony Charges

Ly is charged with felony theft from an elder or dependent adult, grand theft and unauthorized use of personal identifying information.

Prosecutors also filed aggravating factors alleging that the victim was particularly vulnerable, that the offenses involved planning, sophistication or professionalism, and that Ly took advantage of a position of trust.

Ly pleaded not guilty to all counts at his Aug. 18 arraignment. He remains out of custody on $50,000 bail and is scheduled for an early disposition conference in Ventura County Superior Court on Sept. 22. The allegations against him have not been proven in court.

Investigators Believe There Could Be Additional Victims

Authorities say the investigation may extend beyond the 89-year-old man. The Ventura County Sheriff's Office is asking anyone who believes they had a similar experience involving Ly, or who has information that could assist investigators, to contact Senior Deputy Andrew Van Gundy at 805-494-8231.

Someone Helping With a Phone Should Not Need Unrestricted Access to Financial Accounts

The FBI advises older adults not to provide banking or personal information to people they cannot independently verify. Families should also watch for unexplained withdrawals, changes in financial behavior or a new person gaining unusual influence over someone's finances.

When another person needs to troubleshoot a phone, the account owner can unlock the device themselves and remain present rather than giving away the PIN. Banking and cryptocurrency apps should be closed before the device is handed over, and passwords or verification codes should not be shared.

Two-factor authentication can add another barrier if someone obtains a password. The Federal Trade Commission warns that verification codes function as an additional security key and should never be given to another person who wants access to an account. After someone else has had access to a phone containing financial apps, review recent logins and transactions, change any credentials that may have been exposed and contact the financial institution immediately about activity that is not recognized.

Cryptocurrency theft should be reported quickly as well. The FBI recommends providing wallet addresses, transaction amounts, dates and transaction IDs when filing a complaint through its Internet Crime Complaint Center , because those details can help investigators trace where digital assets moved.

articles.title: Helicopter rescue crew caught on camera saving 2 climbers trapped along popular California beach cliff
articles.summary: Video shows a CHP helicopter crew hovering above a Big Sur ravine to hoist two climbers stranded 600 feet below the roadway at Hurricane Point.
articles.body: Two climbers in California stranded on a steep Big Sur cliffside Saturday found themselves 600 feet below the roadway with a California Highway Patrol (CHP) helicopter crew their only way out. Video released by the CHP shows the H-70 helicopter hovering above a steep ravine near Hurricane Point as a rescue technician is lowered on a cable to reach the trapped pair. Big Sur Fire requested help from CHP’s Paso Robles Air Unit at about 6:24 p.m., according to the agency. NOVICE CLIMBER SURVIVES 1,500-FOOT DROP ON CALIFORNIA'S MOUNT SHASTA AFTER HELICOPTER RESCUE DELAYED BY CLOUDS The terrain was so steep that the technician could not safely disconnect from the hoist hook after reaching the first climber. Instead, he secured the climber in a Pelican rescue harness and the two were lifted together to rescue personnel waiting at a staging area. The helicopter then returned to the ravine and carried out the same technical maneuver to bring the second climber to safety. RESCUERS FREE CLIMBER TRAPPED BENEATH 16,000-POUND BOULDER ON OREGON'S MOUNT HOOD IN COMPLEX OPERATION CHP did not release the climbers’ names or explain how they became stranded. Social media users praised the CHP air crew and the rescue teams involved after video of the operation was posted online. "Incredible rescue!! Well done guys!!" one commenter wrote. Another called it an "amazing job by all involved," while another added, "Just incredible, you guys, thanks for what you do!" Both climbers survived the ordeal, authorities said. HIKER AIRLIFTED AFTER TERRIFYING RATTLESNAKE BITE ON REMOTE TRAIL AS INCIDENTS SURGE IN AREA "These high-risk, low-frequency rescues are exactly what CHP Air Operations personnel continuously train for," the agency said. "There is no room for error when operating in steep terrain, under hoist, and in challenging environmental conditions." The cliffside rescue followed two separate Aug. 9 rescue missions for the same H-70 crew. MISSING GRAND CANYON HIKER, 83, RESCUED AFTER GETTING SEPARATED FROM COMPANION The air unit first hoisted an injured 13-year-old hiker from Pinnacles National Park, working with a Paso Robles Fire Department helicopter rescue technician, CHP said. Later that day, the crew pulled a person who suffered severe injuries in a fall from a waterfall in Big Sur Gorge to safety. articles.title: India snake rescue turns fatal after cobra escapes broken box and bites handler
articles.summary: Human settlement, land-use changes, and daily activity can increase encounters with wild animals.
articles.body:
A snake rescue in central India ended in tragedy after 25-year-old snake rescuer Aman Gohiya died from a cobra bite after capturing the animal.

In Dungra village in Mandla district, a cobra bite during a rescue call later proved fatal for Gohiya, according to Bhaskar English .

Gohiya and a companion went to a village 6 kilometers (about 3.7 miles) away from Bichhiya to remove the snake.

The snake rescuer captured the cobra, but the bite occurred afterward. When Gohiya attempted to place the captured snake into a plastic box, it escaped through a damaged section at the back and bit his leg, the outlet reported.

After being taken first to the Bichhiya Community Health Centre, Gohiya was referred to Mandla District Hospital. Mandla District Hospital Civil Surgeon Dr. Vijay Dhurve said MD Medicine specialist Dr. Mohsin supervised his treatment there, but his condition remained critical despite medical care.

Bhaskar English reported that Gohiya attempted to contain the snake, holding the cobra with one hand and the container with the other. The container was reportedly broken, and Gohiya was not wearing protective clothing.

Snake rescues like this often happen in villages and expanding residential areas, where people and wildlife are pushed into closer contact.

When snakes enter homes, farms, or storage spaces, residents may call local rescuers in hopes of preventing harm to both people and the animal.

Human settlement, land-use changes, and daily activity can increase encounters with wild animals. Attacks are often shaped by the ways humans alter habitats and come into closer range of wildlife.
